topics.title: Marketing channels and the value of intermediaries
topics.summary: A marketing channel is the set of people and firms that get a product from its maker to the buyer. Intermediaries such as agents, wholesalers, retailers and distributors earn their place by adding value: they cut the number of transactions, create time, place, form and possession utility, and perform transactional, logistical and facilitating functions. Every channel decision balances cost against level of service.

topics.title: Channel structures and multiple channels
topics.summary: Channels can be direct (no intermediaries) or indirect, and consumer and business markets use different typical structures. Firms also combine channels: dual distribution, strategic channel alliances, multichannel marketing across the marketplace and marketspace, and seamless omni-channel retailing. Global channels add links between and within nations.

topics.title: Vertical marketing systems
topics.summary: A vertical marketing system replaces independent channel members with a professionally managed, centrally coordinated channel. The three types differ by how coordination is achieved: corporate (ownership through forward or backward integration), contractual (voluntary chains, cooperatives and franchises) and administered (the size and influence of one member). A horizontal marketing system, by contrast, links firms at the same level.

topics.title: Choosing and managing channels
topics.summary: Marketers choose channels based on market, product and company factors, then design them around target market coverage (intensive, selective or exclusive), buyer requirements and profitability. Once running, channels must be managed: members are motivated through sources of power, led by a channel captain, evaluated on performance, and watched for vertical and horizontal conflict, including disintermediation.

topics.title: Logistics and supply chain management
topics.summary: Logistics gets the right products to the right place at the right time at the lowest total cost for the level of customer service buyers expect. Supply chain management integrates information and logistics across suppliers, producers and the marketing channel. Key functions are transportation, order processing (EDI), inventory management (JIT, VMI, ECR/QR) and warehousing (including cross-docking), plus reverse logistics and outsourcing to 3PLs.

concepts.term: Marketing channel and intermediaries
concepts.definition: A marketing channel consists of the individuals and firms involved in the process of making a product or service available for use or consumption by consumers or industrial users. Intermediaries are the individuals or firms performing a role in the marketing channel, involved in making a product available.
concepts.explain: The channel is the whole route a product travels from maker to buyer, including every firm that helps along the way. Intermediaries are the in-between members (agents, wholesalers, retailers, distributors). Reaching potential buyers is essential to successful marketing, and buyers benefit from well-structured, efficient distribution systems. Channels can be direct (no intermediaries) or indirect (one or more intermediaries).
concepts.example: A Quebec maple syrup producer sells to a food wholesaler that supplies Sobeys stores, where shoppers buy the syrup. The producer, wholesaler and Sobeys form the marketing channel; the wholesaler and Sobeys are intermediaries.
concepts.contrast: The marketing channel covers the parties that distribute and promote the finished product toward buyers (downstream). The supply chain is broader: it adds the supplier network upstream (raw materials and parts). Logistics is the management of the physical flow, not the set of firms.
concepts.trap: 'Individuals and firms involved in making a product available' = marketing channel. 'Performing a role IN the channel' = intermediaries. If a stem includes raw-material or parts suppliers, it is describing the supply chain, not the marketing channel.
concepts.mnemonic: Channel = the whole pipe; intermediaries = the joints in the pipe.

concepts.term: Two key trade-offs in channel decisions (cost vs level of service; every partner adds value)
concepts.definition: The instructor's framing: every channel decision requires weighing two elements, cost and level of service, and every channel partner must provide value by performing its functions more efficiently or effectively than the producer could alone.
concepts.explain: More service (faster delivery, more outlets, expert advice, after-sale support) usually costs more, so channel design is a balancing act between what buyers expect and what the firm can afford. An intermediary only earns its place, and its margin, if it adds value, for example by reducing contacts, holding inventory or extending credit more cheaply than the producer could. A partner that adds no value is a candidate for removal, but its functions must then be performed by someone else.
concepts.example: A Kelowna winery could ship every order by overnight courier (high service, high cost) or sell through BC Liquor Stores and private wine shops that hold stock locally (lower cost per bottle). Each shop it uses must add value by reaching buyers the winery could not reach as efficiently itself.
concepts.contrast: These two elements are not the three channel design considerations (target market coverage, buyer requirements, profitability), nor the total logistics cost trade-offs (e.g., faster transport vs lower inventory). The instructor's pair is specifically COST and LEVEL OF SERVICE; what every partner must provide is VALUE.
concepts.trap: 'What must every channel partner provide?' = value (not lowest price, not exclusivity, not financing). Distractor pairs such as 'price and promotion' or 'coverage and exclusivity' sound plausible, but the trade-off is cost vs level of service.
concepts.mnemonic: C-S-V: Cost vs Service, and every partner adds Value.

concepts.term: Terms used for marketing intermediaries (Figure 10-1)
concepts.definition: Middleman: another name for intermediary. Agent or broker: an intermediary with legal authority to act on behalf of another channel member (e.g., a manufacturer); does not take title. Wholesaler: sells to other intermediaries, usually retailers (usually consumer goods). Retailer: sells to consumers. Distributor: general term for an intermediary performing a variety of functions (selling, maintaining inventories, extending credit), usually in business markets. Dealer: general term that can mean distributor, retailer or wholesaler.
concepts.explain: Each label tells you WHO the intermediary sells to and WHETHER it owns the goods. Agents and brokers negotiate on someone else's behalf and never take title. Wholesalers sell to businesses that resell (usually retailers), retailers sell to final consumers, and distributors are the business-market version of a full-function intermediary. 'Dealer' and 'middleman' are loose catch-all words.
concepts.example: A Toronto food broker negotiates shelf space for a small salsa maker with Loblaws but never owns the salsa (agent/broker); a wholesaler buys pallets of salsa and resells them to independent grocers (wholesaler); the grocer sells jars to shoppers (retailer).
concepts.contrast: Agent/broker vs wholesaler: the agent does NOT take title; the wholesaler does. Wholesaler vs distributor: 'wholesaler' usually refers to consumer goods sold to other intermediaries, 'distributor' to business markets and many functions. Retailer sells to ultimate consumers; wholesaler sells to other intermediaries.
concepts.trap: 'Legal authority to act on behalf of' or 'does not take title' = agent/broker. 'Sells to other intermediaries, usually retailers' = wholesaler. 'Business market, extends credit, maintains inventory' = distributor. 'Can mean distributor, retailer or wholesaler' = dealer. 'Another name for intermediary' = middleman.
concepts.mnemonic: Agents Act for others (no title); Wholesalers sell to those Who resell; Retailers sell to the Real user.

concepts.term: How intermediaries create value: fewer transactions and utilities
concepts.definition: Intermediaries minimize the number of transactions: without an intermediary every producer must contact every buyer (producers x buyers contacts); with one intermediary each party contacts only the intermediary (producers + buyers contacts). Intermediaries also create time, place, form and possession utility.
concepts.explain: In Figure 10-2, four producers selling to four buyers need 4 x 4 = 16 contacts; routing everything through one intermediary (Best Buy) cuts this to 4 + 4 = 8. Fewer contacts mean lower selling and buying costs for everyone. Intermediaries also make products available when buyers want them (time), where they want them (place), in a usable form (form) and easy to acquire or own, for example through credit (possession).
concepts.example: Five Alberta craft breweries each selling to six Calgary restaurants would need 5 x 6 = 30 relationships; one beverage distributor in between reduces this to 5 + 6 = 11.
concepts.contrast: Contact efficiency is about the NUMBER of transactions, while the channel functions (transactional, logistical, facilitating) are the WORK intermediaries do. Time utility (available when wanted) is not place utility (available where wanted); possession utility is about ease of ownership (credit, transfer of title).
concepts.trap: Calculations: MULTIPLY for no intermediary, ADD for one intermediary; contacts saved = (P x B) - (P + B). Utility cue words: 'when' = time, 'where' = place, 'credit / easy to own' = possession, 'altered or assembled' = form.
concepts.mnemonic: Without = Multiply; With = Add. Utilities: Time, Place, Form, Possession.

concepts.term: Channel functions performed by intermediaries (transactional, logistical, facilitating)
concepts.definition: Intermediaries perform three families of functions. Transactional: buying, selling and risk-taking. Logistical: selection (assorting), storing, sorting and transporting. Facilitating: financing, marketing information and research, and grading.
concepts.explain: Ask what the intermediary is DOING. Ownership and the deal (buying to resell, promoting and seeking orders, bearing the risk that inventory spoils or goes out of style) = transactional. The physical product (gathering an assortment, holding it, breaking bulk, moving it) = logistical. Making the exchange easier without handling the goods or the deal (credit, market intelligence, grading) = facilitating. A producer can eliminate an intermediary but not its functions; someone must still perform them.
concepts.example: A Winnipeg grocery wholesaler buys cereal by the truckload (buying), breaks it into cases for corner stores (sorting), keeps it in its warehouse (storing), delivers it (transporting), lets stores pay in 30 days (financing) and shares sales-trend reports with manufacturers (marketing information and research).
concepts.contrast: Risk-taking is TRANSACTIONAL (it comes from owning inventory), not facilitating. Financing is FACILITATING, not transactional, even though money is involved. Sorting (buy in bulk, divide into smaller amounts) and selection (gather products from several sources) are both LOGISTICAL. 'Informational function' is not one of the three family names.
concepts.trap: Stems mix verbs: a supermarket that 'buys produce from different sources, transfers it to its stores and arranges it' is performing the LOGISTICAL function (assorting, transporting, displaying), even though 'buys' appears. Look for the dominant activity. 'Extends credit' = facilitating; 'promotes and seeks orders' = transactional; 'divides large lots into smaller amounts' = logistical sorting; 'assigns quality grades' = facilitating grading.
concepts.mnemonic: Transactional = BSR (Buy, Sell, Risk). Logistical = Select, Store, Sort, Transport. Facilitating = FIG (Financing, Information, Grading).

concepts.term: Direct vs indirect channels
concepts.definition: A direct channel is one in which the producer and the ultimate consumer deal directly with each other, with no intermediaries. An indirect channel inserts intermediaries (agents, wholesalers, retailers, distributors) between the producer and consumers, and they perform numerous channel functions.
concepts.explain: Direct channels give the producer full control and direct customer contact but force it to perform every channel function itself. Indirect channels hand functions such as storing, sorting, selling and financing to intermediaries that can often perform them more efficiently. Whether the sale happens online is irrelevant: the only test is whether an intermediary sits between producer and consumer.
concepts.example: Mary Kay and Dell sell directly to consumers (direct). A Saskatoon jam maker that sells through a wholesaler to Co-op grocery stores uses an indirect channel.
concepts.contrast: Direct vs indirect is about whether intermediaries exist, not whether the sale is online. A brand selling on its own website is direct; a brand selling through Amazon or Best Buy's website uses an intermediary (indirect). Dual distribution means using BOTH kinds of channel for the same product.
concepts.trap: 'Uses intermediaries like wholesalers and retailers' = indirect. 'Online' is a distractor because online sales can be direct or indirect. Removing intermediaries does not remove their functions; the producer must take them on.
concepts.mnemonic: Direct = nobody in the middle.

concepts.term: Consumer (B2C) channel structures
concepts.definition: Four common consumer channels: A Producer -> Consumer (direct, e.g., Mary Kay, Dell); B Producer -> Retailer -> Consumer (large retailers buying straight from producers, e.g., Walmart, Canadian Tire); C Producer -> Wholesaler -> Retailer -> Consumer (most common for low-cost, low-unit-value items such as candy and magazines); D Producer -> Agent -> Wholesaler -> Retailer -> Consumer (agents bring producers and wholesalers together, e.g., Mars candy).
concepts.explain: Each step from A to D adds one more intermediary. Big retailers buy in volumes large enough to deal straight with producers (B). Low-value items sold in thousands of small stores need a wholesaler to break bulk and reach those stores economically (C). When a producer needs help reaching many wholesalers, an agent, who never takes title, is added in front of the wholesaler (D).
concepts.example: A Winnipeg candy maker selling through a confectionery wholesaler to convenience stores uses channel C; Canadian Tire buying barbecues straight from the manufacturer is channel B.
concepts.contrast: Channel B skips the wholesaler because the retailer is big enough to buy direct; channel C adds a wholesaler for low-unit-value goods sold through many small retailers; channel D adds an agent in front of the wholesaler. The agent does not take title; the wholesaler does. Only channel A is direct.
concepts.trap: Stems describe a situation and ask for the structure or the missing member. 'Large retailer buys direct from the manufacturer' = B; 'candy or magazines through wholesalers to many small stores' = C; 'agent connects producer with wholesalers' = D. Industrial distributors never appear in consumer channels.
concepts.mnemonic: A = Alone (direct), B = Big retailer, C = Candy through a wholesaler, D = aDD an agent.

concepts.term: Business (B2B) channel structures and industrial distributors
concepts.definition: Four common business channels: A Producer -> Industrial user (direct, e.g., IBM); B Producer -> Industrial distributor -> Industrial user (e.g., Caterpillar); C Producer -> Agent -> Industrial user; D Producer -> Agent -> Industrial distributor -> Industrial user. An industrial distributor performs functions similar to a wholesaler in business markets; agents do not take title or physical possession of the goods.
concepts.explain: Business channels tend to be shorter than consumer channels because buyers are fewer and larger and often need technical selling. Direct (A) suits expensive, complex products sold to a few large buyers. Industrial distributors (B) stock and resell standardized items and equipment to many users. Agents (C) represent the producer in negotiations without owning or holding goods, which is useful when the firm lacks its own sales force; adding a distributor after the agent (D) supplies inventory and local delivery.
concepts.example: A Calgary valve maker sells custom valves directly to a large oil sands producer (A) but sells standard fittings through an industrial supply distributor to hundreds of small contractors (B).
concepts.contrast: Industrial distributor = the B2B equivalent of a wholesaler (takes title, holds inventory). Agent = no title and no physical possession. Consumer channels end with a consumer and can include retailers; business channels end with an industrial user and never include a retailer.
concepts.trap: 'Industrial distributor' only appears in business channels. If a stem says the intermediary 'never handles the goods' or 'earns a commission for arranging sales', it is an agent, not a distributor.
concepts.mnemonic: B2B: the Distributor stocks and Delivers; the Agent only Arranges.

concepts.term: Electronic and direct marketing channels (and e-commerce trends)
concepts.definition: Electronic marketing channels use the Internet to make goods and services available to consumers or business buyers (e.g., Amazon, Expedia). Direct marketing channels allow consumers to buy products by interacting with various advertising media without a face-to-face meeting with a salesperson (catalogues, telemarketing, direct mail, TV home shopping, online).
concepts.explain: Electronic channels can perform many channel functions online; Expedia, for example, is an intermediary between travellers and airlines or hotels. Direct marketing channels are about buying through a medium (catalogue, phone, mail, TV, screen) rather than through a person. The instructor's e-commerce trends slide adds: top categories are fashion and electronics; AI personalization, AR and VR; CRM and customer support; hybrid commerce; multiple payment options such as buy now, pay later; voice activation; social selling; data privacy; sustainability; and fast, free delivery.
concepts.example: Expedia (electronic marketing channel) lets travellers book flights and hotels from many suppliers; a TV shopping channel where viewers phone in orders is a direct marketing channel.
concepts.contrast: An electronic channel can be indirect (Expedia and Amazon are intermediaries), so 'online' does not automatically mean 'direct channel'. A direct MARKETING channel (buying through media without a salesperson) differs from a DIRECT CHANNEL (no intermediaries): a TV shopping network selling many brands is direct marketing but is still an intermediary.
concepts.trap: 'Without a face-to-face meeting with a salesperson', catalogue, telemarketing or TV home shopping = direct marketing channel. 'Uses the Internet to make goods available' = electronic marketing channel. In trends questions, options like 'dropping free delivery' or 'eliminating customer support' are the planted wrong answers.
concepts.mnemonic: Electronic = Internet; direct MARKETING = Media, no salesperson.

concepts.term: Dual distribution
concepts.definition: Dual distribution is an arrangement whereby a firm reaches buyers by using two or more different types of channels for the same basic product.
concepts.explain: Dual distribution lets a firm reach different segments, for example large accounts through its own sales force and small ones through distributors, or shoppers through both retailers and its own website. A website can play several roles at once: transactional (taking orders) and promotional (information and brand building). The main risk is conflict when the channels compete for the same customers.
concepts.example: Prairie Peak Outerwear (a fictional Alberta brand) sells the same parkas through Sport Chek stores and through its own online store.
concepts.contrast: Dual distribution = ONE firm using two or more of its own channel TYPES for the same product. Strategic channel alliance = one firm's products sold through ANOTHER firm's channel. Multichannel marketing = blending communication AND delivery channels so they reinforce each other. Omni-channel = a seamless experience across channels. Intensive/selective/exclusive = number of outlets, not channel types.
concepts.trap: Cue: 'same basic product' + 'two or more different types of channels'. If the stem stresses mutual reinforcement of communication and delivery channels, think multichannel; if it stresses a seamless customer experience, think omni-channel; if another company's channel is used, think strategic alliance.
concepts.mnemonic: Dual = same product, two channel types.

concepts.term: Strategic channel alliances
concepts.definition: A strategic channel alliance is an arrangement whereby one firm's marketing channel is used to sell another firm's products.
concepts.explain: Instead of building its own distribution, a firm borrows a partner's established channel. This gives quick, low-cost access to buyers, as when Starbucks coffee is sold in Safeway. The partner benefits by adding products its customers want. No ownership is involved.
concepts.example: Starbucks coffee sold in Safeway stores; a small B.C. kombucha brand delivered and sold by a national juice company's trucks and sales force.
concepts.contrast: Dual distribution = one firm using its own two or more channel types. Strategic channel alliance = one firm's channel sells another firm's products. Horizontal marketing system = unrelated firms at the same level pooling resources. Franchising = a contractual VMS. Owning the partner's outlets = corporate VMS.
concepts.trap: Cue: 'one firm's channel is used to sell another firm's products' or 'uses a partner's distribution network'. If no second company's channel is involved, it is not an alliance.
concepts.mnemonic: Alliance = borrow a partner's channel.

concepts.term: Multichannel marketing (marketplace vs marketspace) and omni-channel retailing
concepts.definition: Multichannel marketing is the blending of different communication and delivery channels that are mutually reinforcing in attracting, retaining and building relationships with consumers who shop in the traditional marketplace (face-to-face) and the online marketspace (face-to-screen). Omni-channel retailing creates a seamless shopping experience among all available shopping channels (online, catalogue, in-store).
concepts.explain: Multichannel marketing uses several channels (stores, catalogues, websites, apps) that support each other, leveraging the value-adding capabilities of each: the store lets people touch the product, the website offers convenience and information. Omni-channel retailing goes a step further: the customer experiences all channels as one seamless system, with a shared cart, inventory, loyalty account and returns.
concepts.example: A shopper checks stock on a retailer's app, buys online, picks up in store and returns the item at a different location, all as one continuous omni-channel experience.
concepts.contrast: Omni-channel is NOT just another term for multichannel marketing (official question). Multichannel = several mutually reinforcing channels; omni = those channels feel like one seamless experience. Dual distribution = two channel types for the same product, with no requirement that they be integrated.
concepts.trap: 'Seamless' = omni-channel. 'Mutually reinforcing communication and delivery channels' or 'leverage the value-adding capabilities of each' = multichannel. 'Face-to-face' = marketplace; 'face-to-screen' = marketspace.
concepts.mnemonic: Omni = One seamless experience. MarketPLACE = a physical place; MarketSPACE = cyberSPACE.

concepts.term: Global channel strategy (Figure 10-7)
concepts.definition: In global marketing the channel runs Seller -> Seller's international marketing headquarters -> Channels between nations -> Channels within foreign nations -> Final consumer. Channel sophistication increases as a country's economic infrastructure develops.
concepts.explain: The international marketing headquarters manages the global effort; channels between nations move the product across borders (e.g., export agents, freight forwarders); channels within foreign nations distribute it inside the market (local wholesalers and retailers). Where economic infrastructure is less developed, intermediaries are fewer and less specialized, so marketers must adapt.
concepts.example: A Banff skincare brand's international marketing team ships through an export agent and freight forwarder (between nations) to a Tokyo wholesaler that supplies department stores (within the foreign nation), which sell to Japanese consumers.
concepts.contrast: Channels BETWEEN nations (crossing borders) vs channels WITHIN foreign nations (local distribution inside the market). Global channel strategy is about the sequence of links across countries, not about the number of channel types (dual distribution) or blending channels (multichannel).
concepts.trap: Order questions: immediately after the international marketing headquarters = channels between nations; immediately before the final consumer = channels within foreign nations. Sophistication grows with economic infrastructure, not with distance or population.
concepts.mnemonic: Seller, HQ, Between, Within, Consumer: 'Sellers Head Beyond borders, Within markets, to Consumers.'

concepts.term: Vertical marketing systems (VMS) vs horizontal marketing systems
concepts.definition: Vertical marketing systems are professionally managed and centrally coordinated marketing channels designed to achieve channel economies and maximum marketing impact. The three types are corporate (ownership), contractual (contracts) and administered (size and influence of one member). Contrast: a horizontal marketing system is two or more unrelated companies at the same channel level pooling resources.
concepts.explain: In a conventional channel each member acts independently to maximize its own profit; a VMS coordinates the levels (producer, wholesaler, retailer) as one system. The three types differ only in HOW that coordination is achieved. 'Vertical' means up and down the levels; 'horizontal' means side by side at the same level.
concepts.example: Apple Stores (corporate), IGA and Home Hardware (contractual), Procter & Gamble's influence over retailers (administered); two unrelated producers sharing a delivery van (horizontal marketing system, not a VMS).
concepts.contrast: VMS coordinates DIFFERENT levels; a horizontal marketing system combines firms at the SAME level. Within VMS: corporate (owns), contractual (signs), administered (dominates).
concepts.trap: Cue: 'professionally managed and centrally coordinated' = VMS. 'Two or more unrelated companies at the same level pool resources' = horizontal marketing system, a frequent distractor (e.g., in the Mocha Jive official question). 'Horizontal' is never one of the three VMS types.
concepts.mnemonic: Own it, Sign it, or Sway it: Corporate, Contractual, Administered.

concepts.term: Corporate VMS (forward and backward integration)
concepts.definition: A corporate VMS combines successive stages of production and distribution under a single ownership. Forward integration: a producer owns intermediaries downstream (e.g., Apple Stores, Ralph Lauren's Polo stores). Backward integration: a retailer or wholesaler owns upstream manufacturing or wholesaling (e.g., a coffee chain owning the bakery that makes its cookies).
concepts.explain: One company owns two or more successive levels of the channel, so it can coordinate them directly. Integration can go forward (toward the consumer) or backward (toward the source). Ownership gives maximum control but requires major investment.
concepts.example: Ralph Lauren operating its own Polo stores and Apple running Apple Stores (forward integration); Mocha Jive coffee shops owning Perfect Cookies, which bakes for its cafés (backward integration).
concepts.contrast: Forward = toward the consumer (a manufacturer owns stores); backward = toward the source (a retailer owns its supplier). Corporate (ownership) vs contractual (independent firms bound by contracts, e.g., franchises) vs administered (no ownership, no contract, only influence).
concepts.trap: Ask which direction the OWNER is reaching. Coffee shop owning its cookie maker = backward (official question). Designer opening its own boutiques = forward. Buying from a supplier without owning it is not integration. A franchise is contractual, not corporate.
concepts.mnemonic: Forward = toward the Front door (consumer); Backward = Back toward the factory.

concepts.term: Contractual VMS (voluntary chains, cooperatives, franchises)
concepts.definition: A contractual VMS is one in which independently owned firms at different levels of production and distribution integrate their efforts on a contractual basis to obtain greater functional economies and marketing impact than they could alone. Forms: wholesaler-sponsored voluntary chains (IGA), retailer-sponsored cooperatives (Home Hardware) and franchise programs (manufacturer-sponsored retail, manufacturer-sponsored wholesale, service-sponsored retail, service-sponsored franchise systems).
concepts.explain: Firms stay independently owned but sign agreements that coordinate buying, merchandising and branding. The voluntary chain vs cooperative distinction is about who starts it: a WHOLESALER signs up independent retailers (voluntary chain), or independent RETAILERS band together to run their own wholesale operation (cooperative). Franchises are classified by who sponsors them (a manufacturer or a service company) and at what level (retail or wholesale).
concepts.example: IGA grocers coordinated by a wholesaler (voluntary chain); Home Hardware stores that jointly own their wholesale operation (cooperative); Ford dealers, Coca-Cola bottlers, Canadian Tire, H&R Block, Holiday Inn and McDonald's (franchises).
concepts.contrast: Voluntary chain (wholesaler-sponsored) vs cooperative (retailer-sponsored). Manufacturer-sponsored RETAIL franchise (Ford dealers sell to consumers) vs manufacturer-sponsored WHOLESALE franchise (Coca-Cola bottlers sell to retailers). Contractual (independent owners plus contracts) vs corporate (one owner) vs administered (influence only).
concepts.trap: IGA = wholesaler-sponsored voluntary chain; Home Hardware = retailer-sponsored cooperative. Coca-Cola bottlers = manufacturer-sponsored WHOLESALE franchise. A franchise system looks like one company, but it is CONTRACTUAL, not corporate.
concepts.mnemonic: Voluntary chain = a Wholesaler woos retailers; Cooperative = retailers Club together.

concepts.term: Administered VMS
concepts.definition: An administered VMS achieves coordination at successive stages of production and distribution through the size and influence of one channel member, rather than through ownership or contracts (e.g., Procter & Gamble, Walmart).
concepts.explain: No one owns anyone and no franchise-type contract binds them, yet the channel behaves as a coordinated system because one member is so large and important that the others go along with its programs (displays, pricing, inventory systems). It rests on channel power.
concepts.example: Procter & Gamble gets retailers to cooperate on displays and promotions; Walmart's buying power leads suppliers to adopt its inventory and delivery systems.
concepts.contrast: Administered (influence, no ownership, no contract) vs corporate (ownership) vs contractual (formal agreements such as franchises, voluntary chains, cooperatives).
concepts.trap: Cue: 'because of its size or market power, it gets others to cooperate' with no ownership and no contract = administered. 'Administered' here has nothing to do with government administration.
concepts.mnemonic: Administered = Authority by size (no deed, no contract).

concepts.term: Factors affecting channel choice (market, product, company)
concepts.definition: Market factors: geographic concentration, number of potential customers, type of market (consumer vs business) and order size. Product factors: technical factors, perishability, unit value and product life cycle stage. Company factors: financial resources and ability of management, and desire for channel control.
concepts.explain: Market factors ask who and where the buyers are; product factors ask what is being sold; company factors ask what the firm can afford and how much control it wants. Rules of thumb: few, concentrated buyers placing large orders -> shorter or direct channels; many dispersed buyers placing small orders -> indirect. Technical or perishable products -> short or direct; low unit value -> long and indirect. Strong resources and a strong desire for control -> direct.
concepts.example: Live Nova Scotia lobster (perishable) moves through a short channel; a granola bar (low unit value, millions of buyers) moves through wholesalers and retailers.
concepts.contrast: Keep the groups straight: geographic concentration, number of customers, type of market and order size are MARKET factors; technical factors, perishability, unit value and PLC stage are PRODUCT factors; financial resources/management ability and desire for control are COMPANY factors. These differ from the three channel design considerations (coverage, buyer requirements, profitability).
concepts.trap: Questions ask you to classify a factor or predict channel length. 'Perishability' is a product factor (not a transportation criterion); 'order size' is a market factor (not a product factor); 'desire for control' is a company factor.
concepts.mnemonic: Market = who, where, how many, how much; Product = tech, spoil, value, life cycle; Company = cash and control.

concepts.term: Target market coverage: intensive, selective and exclusive distribution
concepts.definition: Intensive distribution places products in as many outlets as possible (convenience goods). Selective distribution uses a few retailers in a specific geographic area (shopping goods such as appliances and apparel). Exclusive distribution uses only one retailer in a specific geographic area (specialty goods such as luxury cars, yachts and some fragrances).
concepts.explain: Coverage answers 'how many outlets in an area?' Convenience goods are bought often with little effort, so they must be everywhere (intensive). Shopping goods are compared across a few stores (selective). Specialty goods are sought out by brand-loyal buyers, so one dealer per area is enough and protects image and service (exclusive).
concepts.example: Gum and soft drinks in every gas station and grocery store (intensive); appliances at a few Edmonton retailers (selective); one luxury sports car dealer in Calgary (exclusive).
concepts.contrast: Intensive vs selective vs exclusive = number of outlets per area. Dual distribution = number of channel TYPES, not coverage intensity, even though it also ends in 'distribution'.
concepts.trap: Cue words: 'as many outlets as possible' = intensive; 'a few retailers in an area' = selective; 'only one retailer in a specified geographic area' = exclusive. Product cues: convenience -> intensive, shopping -> selective, specialty -> exclusive. 'Dual distribution' is a planted distractor (official question 1).
concepts.mnemonic: Convenience-Intensive, Shopping-Selective, Specialty-Exclusive (C-I, S-S, S-E).

concepts.term: Channel design: buyer requirements and profitability
concepts.definition: Besides target market coverage, channel design considers (2) satisfying buyer requirements: information, convenience, variety, and pre- and/or post-sale services; and (3) profitability: each channel's distribution, advertising and selling expenses relative to the revenue and margins it generates.
concepts.explain: Information: buyers of technical or unfamiliar products need knowledgeable salespeople. Convenience: easy-to-reach locations, longer hours, online ordering, pickup options. Variety: breadth and depth of assortment. Pre- and post-sale services: delivery, installation, repair, training, maintenance. Profitability: a channel that satisfies buyers but loses money for its members will not last.
concepts.example: A Calgary hot-tub dealer that delivers, installs and services every tub meets post-sale service requirements, but the channel must still be profitable once its distribution, advertising and selling costs are counted.
concepts.contrast: Coverage = how many outlets; buyer requirements = what buyers need from the channel; profitability = whether the channel makes money. Buyer requirements are not the transportation criteria (cost, time, capability, dependability, accessibility, frequency) or the criteria for evaluating channel members (sales, inventory levels, treatment of damaged goods).
concepts.trap: List cues: 'information, convenience, variety, pre- and post-sale services' = buyer requirements; 'distribution, advertising and selling expenses' = profitability. A scenario where customers are delighted but members lose money is a profitability failure, not a buyer-requirements failure.
concepts.mnemonic: ICVS: Information, Convenience, Variety, Service; then ask, is it Profitable?

concepts.term: Channel power, the channel captain and evaluating channel members
concepts.definition: Channel members are motivated through sources of power: coercive (threat of punishment or withdrawal of support), reward (incentives), legitimate (authority from position or contract), expert (specialized knowledge others value) and referent (others want to be identified with a respected member). A channel captain is a channel member that coordinates, directs and supports other members; it can be a producer, wholesaler or retailer (e.g., Walmart). Members are evaluated on sales, inventory levels, treatment of damaged/lost goods and others (customer service, cooperation in promotion).
concepts.explain: Channel members are independent businesses, so the stronger ones motivate the others with power. Coercive (sticks) and reward (carrots) are the most direct; legitimate power comes from a formal position or contract; expert power from know-how; referent power from others wanting to be associated with a respected brand. The member that uses its power to lead the channel is the channel captain. At review time, members are judged on sales, inventory levels, how they treat damaged or lost goods, and other factors such as customer service and promotional cooperation.
concepts.example: Walmart acts as channel captain, using its buying power to set delivery and inventory standards for its suppliers.
concepts.contrast: Coercive (threat) vs reward (incentive): same goal, opposite tools. Legitimate (contract or position) vs referent (admiration). Expert (knowledge) vs referent (identification). Channel captain is a ROLE (leader of the channel); power is the means it uses.
concepts.trap: 'Or we will stop supplying you' = coercive; 'bonus or allowance' = reward; 'the agreement entitles us' = legitimate; 'because of their know-how' = expert; 'want to be associated with the prestige' = referent. The channel captain does not have to be the manufacturer.
concepts.mnemonic: Stick, Carrot, Contract, Know-how, Admiration = Coercive, Reward, Legitimate, Expert, Referent.

concepts.term: Channel conflict: vertical vs horizontal
concepts.definition: Channel conflict arises when one channel member believes another channel member is engaged in behaviour that prevents it from achieving its goals. Vertical conflict occurs between different levels of a marketing channel (e.g., manufacturer vs wholesaler or retailer). Horizontal conflict occurs between intermediaries at the same level (e.g., two dealers of the same brand).
concepts.explain: Channel members are independent businesses with their own goals, so friction is natural. Conflict is vertical when it runs up and down the channel: a producer arguing with its wholesaler over price, squeezing retailers' margins, or bypassing them (disintermediation). It is horizontal when it is between members at the same level, such as two dealers of the same brand fighting over territory.
concepts.example: Tez energy drinks arguing with a major wholesaler over price (vertical); two Edmonton dealers of the same truck brand poaching each other's customers (horizontal).
concepts.contrast: Vertical = different levels; horizontal = same level. Disintermediation is a specific cause of vertical conflict (bypassing a member), not a synonym for channel conflict in general.
concepts.trap: Check the LEVELS of the two parties named in the stem. Producer vs wholesaler or retailer = vertical, whatever the topic (price, territory, margins), and a producer bypassing a member to sell direct is disintermediation (vertical). One course nuance: the slides list a retailer competing with the maker's own online store under dual distribution as a horizontal-conflict example, because both outlets compete at the retail level. Retailer vs retailer of the same brand = horizontal. 'Selective conflict' and 'disintegration' are not real terms.
concepts.mnemonic: Vertical = up and down the ladder; Horizontal = across the same rung.

concepts.term: Disintermediation
concepts.definition: Disintermediation is a channel conflict that arises when a channel member bypasses another member and sells or buys products directly from others (e.g., a manufacturer selling direct to consumers online, bypassing its retailers).
concepts.explain: Disintermediation literally means removing the intermediary. A manufacturer might start selling directly online, cutting out retailers who then feel threatened; or a large buyer might stop using a distributor and buy straight from producers. Because the parties are at different levels, it is a form of vertical conflict. The bypassed member's functions do not disappear; someone else must now perform them.
concepts.example: A mattress maker that always sold through furniture stores launches a direct-to-consumer website, and its retailers protest.
concepts.contrast: Disintermediation (bypassing a member, no ownership) vs forward/backward integration (owning another stage) vs dual distribution (adding a second channel type, which can trigger disintermediation-type conflict) vs horizontal conflict (members at the same level).
concepts.trap: Cue: 'bypasses', 'cuts out the middleman', 'sells or buys directly instead of through'. It works on the buying side too. Do not choose horizontal conflict, because the bypassed member is at a different level.
concepts.mnemonic: Dis-INTERMEDIARY-ation = taking the intermediary out.

concepts.term: Logistics, customer service and total logistics cost
concepts.definition: Logistics: activities that focus on getting the right amount of the right products to the right place at the right time at the lowest possible cost. Logistics is built around the expected level of customer service (time or order cycle, dependability, communication, convenience) and aims to minimize total logistics cost: the expenses of transportation, materials handling and warehousing, inventory, stockouts, order processing, and return goods handling.
concepts.explain: Logistics requires collaboration, coordination and information sharing among manufacturers, suppliers and distributors so the flow is seamless. Its costs trade off against each other: faster shipping raises transportation cost but can lower inventory and stockout costs; fewer warehouses lower warehousing cost but raise transport cost. The goal is the lowest TOTAL cost for the level of service customers expect, not the lowest cost of any single activity. The four key logistics functions are transportation, order processing, inventory management and warehousing.
concepts.example: A Calgary office-supply distributor promises next-day delivery (time), meets that promise 99% of the time (dependability), sends tracking alerts (communication) and offers easy online ordering (convenience), while weighing faster trucking costs against lower inventory costs.
concepts.contrast: Logistics (moving goods efficiently) vs supply chain management (integrating information and logistics across all firms in the chain) vs marketing channel (the parties that distribute and promote). Within customer service, 'time' is the order cycle or lead time, while 'dependability' is how consistently that time is met.
concepts.trap: Definition cue: 'right amount, right products, right place, right time, lowest possible cost' = logistics. Total cost questions: add every cost that changes (transportation, warehousing, inventory, stockouts, order processing, returns) and never judge by one cost alone. Advertising is not a logistics cost.
concepts.mnemonic: Four rights at the lowest cost; service = Time, Dependability, Communication, Convenience.

concepts.term: Supply chain management (supply chain vs marketing channel, Figure 10-9)
concepts.definition: Supply chain management is the integration and organization of information and logistics activities across firms in a supply chain for the purpose of creating and delivering goods and services that provide value to consumers. A supply chain runs Suppliers -> Producer -> Consumers and includes the supplier network (all parties supplying raw materials and parts) plus the marketing channel (all parties involved in distributing and promoting the product).
concepts.explain: The supply chain is the whole sequence from raw-material suppliers through the producer to consumers. SCM manages it as one system, sharing information (forecasts, inventory data) and coordinating logistics across company lines. The marketing channel is only the downstream part; the supplier network is the upstream part. The supply chain must be harmonized with the marketing strategy, built to deliver the value the target market expects.
concepts.example: A bike maker shares real-time sales data and forecasts with its tire suppliers and its retailers so that production and deliveries match demand.
concepts.contrast: Supply chain (supplier network + producer + marketing channel) vs marketing channel (distributing and promoting only). Logistics management coordinates the movement of goods throughout; supply chain management integrates information AND logistics across all parties.
concepts.trap: If a stem mentions raw-material or parts suppliers, it is describing the supply chain, not just the marketing channel. 'Integration and organization of information and logistics activities across firms' = SCM; 'right products, right place, right time, lowest cost' = logistics.
concepts.mnemonic: Supply chain = Supplier network + Marketing channel.

concepts.term: Transportation: criteria and modes
concepts.definition: Transportation alternatives are evaluated on six criteria: cost, time, capability, dependability, accessibility and frequency. The modes are rail, truck, air, water, pipeline and intermodal (combinations of modes).
concepts.explain: Cost = what the carrier charges; time = speed of delivery; capability = ability to provide the right equipment and conditions (e.g., refrigeration, oversized loads); dependability = reliability in delivering on time without loss or damage; accessibility = ability to reach the needed locations or routes; frequency = how often shipments can be scheduled. Air is fastest but costliest; water and rail move bulky goods cheaply but slowly; trucks are flexible and accessible; pipelines carry liquids and gases; intermodal combines modes.
concepts.example: A vaccine maker that needs -20 C refrigeration focuses on capability; a jeweller shipping small, high-value parcels across the country chooses air for speed.
concepts.contrast: Capability (right equipment) vs accessibility (can reach the place); dependability (consistency) vs frequency (how often). Transportation criteria differ from the product factors in channel choice (perishability, unit value).
concepts.trap: Swapped definitions are the main trick. 'Perishability' is a channel-choice product factor, not one of the six transportation criteria. Intermodal is a combination of modes, not a warehousing practice like cross-docking.
concepts.mnemonic: 'Can The Carrier Deliver Any Freight?' = Cost, Time, Capability, Dependability, Accessibility, Frequency.

concepts.term: Order processing (EDI) and inventory management (JIT, VMI, ECR/QR)
concepts.definition: Order processing increasingly uses electronic data interchange (EDI): computers in different firms exchange documents such as purchase orders and invoices electronically. Firms hold inventory to buffer variations in supply and demand, provide better service, promote efficiency and speculate. Just-in-time (JIT): an inventory supply system with very low inventories that requires fast, on-time delivery; suppliers deliver less merchandise more frequently. Vendor-managed inventory (VMI): the supplier determines the product amount and assortment a customer needs and automatically delivers it. Efficient consumer response (ECR) / quick response (QR): inventory management systems designed to reduce the retailer's lead time for receiving merchandise, lowering inventory investment and improving customer service.
concepts.explain: Inventory is useful but expensive, so modern systems try to keep less of it without running out. EDI speeds up and automates ordering. JIT shrinks stock by having suppliers deliver small amounts often. VMI hands the reorder decision to the supplier. ECR/QR shortens how long a retailer waits for replenishment, so it can carry less stock while keeping shelves full.
concepts.example: A pharmacy whose supplier reads its sales data and restocks automatically (VMI); a car plant receiving parts several times a day (JIT); a hardware chain exchanging purchase orders and invoices computer-to-computer (EDI).
concepts.contrast: JIT = low inventory, small and frequent deliveries; VMI = the SUPPLIER decides and replenishes; ECR/QR = shorten the RETAILER's lead time; EDI = electronic exchange of order documents; cross-docking = a warehousing practice with little or no storage.
concepts.trap: 'Less merchandise on a more frequent basis' = JIT (official question). 'Supplier determines amount and assortment and automatically delivers' = VMI. 'Computer-to-computer purchase orders and invoices' = EDI. 'Reduce the retailer's lead time' = ECR/QR. Do not pick 'time utility' just because JIT is about timing.
concepts.mnemonic: JIT = Just In Time; VMI = the Vendor Minds the Inventory; EDI = Electronic Documents Instantly.

concepts.term: Warehousing: public vs private, storage warehouses vs distribution centres, cross-docking
concepts.definition: Warehouses can be public (space and services rented from independent operators) or private (owned or operated by the firm), or a combination. Traditional storage warehouses hold goods for moderate to long periods; distribution centres are designed to facilitate the timely movement of goods. Cross-docking unloads inbound shipments and loads them onto outbound vehicles with little or no storage.
concepts.explain: The ownership decision (public vs private) is separate from the purpose decision (store vs keep moving). Public space suits seasonal or uncertain needs; private space suits steady, high volumes. Distribution centres and cross-docking keep products flowing quickly toward customers, which reduces inventory.
concepts.example: A grocery chain's distribution centre cross-docks produce from inbound trucks to store-bound trucks within hours; a toy company rents public warehouse space only for the Christmas peak.
concepts.contrast: Storage warehouse (hold) vs distribution centre (move). Public (rent) vs private (own). Cross-docking (warehousing practice) vs JIT (inventory system) vs VMI (who decides replenishment).
concepts.trap: 'Little or no storage' or 'straight from the inbound to the outbound dock' = cross-docking. 'Rent space from an independent operator' = public warehouse. Long-term holding = storage warehouse, not distribution centre.
concepts.mnemonic: Storage warehouse = Store; Distribution centre = Dispatch.

concepts.term: Reverse logistics
concepts.definition: Reverse logistics is a process of reclaiming recyclable and reusable materials, returns and reworks from the point of consumption or use for repair, remanufacturing, redistribution or disposal.
concepts.explain: Most logistics moves goods forward to the customer; reverse logistics moves them back: returns, worn-out products, packaging and recyclable materials, so they can be repaired, remanufactured, redistributed or disposed of responsibly. It recovers value and supports sustainability goals.
concepts.example: H&M accepts used clothing in its stores and recycles it into new textiles.
concepts.contrast: Reverse logistics (products flowing back FROM the consumer) vs backward integration (OWNERSHIP of upstream suppliers) vs disintermediation (bypassing a channel member).
concepts.trap: Pick the option where products flow back from the point of consumption. Shipping to customers, buying from local farmers or a promotional event are forward-channel or promotion activities (official question 8).
concepts.mnemonic: Reverse = back from the customer: Return, Repair, Remanufacture, Recycle.

concepts.term: Third-party logistics providers (3PLs)
concepts.definition: Third-party logistics providers are firms that perform most or all of the logistics functions that manufacturers, suppliers and distributors would normally perform themselves.
concepts.explain: Many firms outsource logistics (warehousing, transportation, order fulfilment, returns) to specialists that serve many clients and can do the work more efficiently. This follows the principle that whoever performs a channel function should add value; the functions are still performed, just by a specialist.
concepts.example: An online clothing start-up hands warehousing, order picking, shipping and returns to an outside logistics firm that serves dozens of brands.
concepts.contrast: 3PL (logistics service for a fee, typically without taking title) vs wholesaler or distributor (takes title and resells) vs agent or broker (negotiates sales) vs VMI (supplier manages a customer's inventory) vs strategic channel alliance (selling through another firm's marketing channel).
concepts.trap: Cue: 'an outside firm performs most or all logistics functions for other firms'. Do not confuse with a strategic channel alliance, which is about selling, not outsourcing logistics.
concepts.mnemonic: Third party = a logistics specialist that is neither the buyer nor the seller.

questions.stem: The individuals and firms involved in the process of making a product or service available for use or consumption by consumers or industrial users make up a:
questions.explanation: This is the textbook definition of a marketing channel. 'Supply chain' is tempting but broader: it also includes the supplier network of raw-material and parts suppliers upstream of the producer.

questions.stem: Northern Harvest, a Nova Scotia blueberry grower, sells frozen berries through a food broker, who arranges sales to a wholesaler, which supplies Sobeys stores. In channel terms, the broker, the wholesaler and Sobeys are all:
questions.explanation: Intermediaries are individuals or firms performing a role in the marketing channel, involved in making a product available. These firms are downstream of the grower, so they are not the supplier network (which provides raw materials and parts), and nothing says any of them leads the whole channel.

questions.stem: Velo Laurentien, a Quebec bicycle maker, buys steel tubing from a mill and sells finished bikes through sporting goods retailers. Which statement correctly separates its marketing channel from its supply chain?
options: The retailers are part of the supply chain but not the marketing channel; the mill is part of both
The marketing channel and the supply chain are identical and include exactly the same firms
The mill is part of the supply chain but not the marketing channel; the retailers are part of both
Only the mill and the bike maker belong to the marketing channel
questions.explanation: In Figure 10-9 the supply chain = supplier network (raw materials and parts, like the mill) + marketing channel (parties that distribute and promote the product, like retailers). So retailers sit in both, while the mill sits only in the supply chain.

questions.stem: According to the chapter, why do buyers benefit from a well-structured, efficient marketing channel?
options: A longer channel always lowers the final price because each intermediary adds a discount
It makes products available where and when buyers want them while keeping the cost of reaching them down
It removes the need for channel functions such as storing and transporting
It guarantees that every product is sold directly by its producer
questions.explanation: Reaching buyers efficiently is the point of a channel: intermediaries cut the number of contacts and perform functions that make products conveniently available. Channel functions never disappear, and efficient channels are often indirect rather than direct.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an intermediary in the marketing channel of Crunchwell, a Manitoba snack maker?
options: The farm co-operative that supplies Crunchwell with corn and sunflower oil
The food broker that negotiates listings with grocery chains on Crunchwell's behalf
The wholesaler that resells cases of Crunchwell snacks to convenience stores
The grocery chain that sells Crunchwell snacks to shoppers
questions.explanation: A raw-material supplier belongs to the supplier network (the upstream part of the supply chain), not the marketing channel. The broker, wholesaler and grocer all help make the finished snack available to buyers, so they are intermediaries.

questions.stem: In the instructor's framing of channel decisions, which two elements must always be traded off against each other?
questions.explanation: The instructor's 'two key trade-offs' are cost and level of service: more service (speed, more outlets, support) usually costs more. Coverage (intensive, selective, exclusive) is a separate channel design consideration.

questions.stem: The instructor asks, 'What must every channel partner provide?' The answer is _____: an intermediary earns its place only if it performs its functions more efficiently or effectively than the producer could alone.
questions.explanation: Every channel partner must add value. Financing is one function some partners provide, but not every partner must provide it; exclusivity and ownership are not requirements of channel membership.

questions.stem: Glacier Gear, an Edmonton maker of ski goggles, can ship every online order overnight from its own warehouse with a personal follow-up call, or sell through regional sporting goods stores that hold stock. The overnight option delights customers but costs far more per unit. Which instructor concept is Glacier Gear wrestling with?
options: The choice between forward and backward integration
The difference between vertical and horizontal conflict
The choice between selective and exclusive distribution
The trade-off between cost and level of service
questions.explanation: Higher service (overnight shipping, personal follow-up) comes at a higher cost, which is the instructor's core channel trade-off. Integration would mean owning another channel stage, and selective vs exclusive concerns how many outlets per area, neither of which is the dilemma described.

questions.stem: A Regina furniture maker reviews the regional wholesaler that buys, warehouses and resells its products to retailers. It finds it could do the same storage and delivery itself at lower cost and with better service to the same retailers. Based on the instructor's channel principle, what follows?
options: The wholesaler must be kept, because every channel needs at least one wholesaler
The maker should grant the wholesaler exclusive distribution to motivate it
The wholesaler is not adding value, so the maker should consider taking over its functions
Once the wholesaler is removed, its storage and delivery functions will no longer be needed
questions.explanation: Every channel partner must provide value; if the producer can perform the functions more efficiently, the intermediary is a candidate for removal. The functions themselves never vanish: the maker would now perform the storage and delivery.

questions.stem: Which statement about the instructor's key channel trade-offs is NOT correct?
options: Raising the level of service usually raises channel cost
Every channel partner is expected to add value
Channel choices balance what buyers expect against what it costs to provide it
The lowest-cost channel is always the best choice, regardless of the service buyers expect
questions.explanation: Channel design balances cost against level of service; choosing purely on lowest cost ignores the service side of the trade-off. The other statements restate the instructor's two trade-offs and the value requirement.

questions.stem: Coastal Reps, a Vancouver firm, negotiates sales of a seafood processor's products to restaurant chains and earns a commission. It has legal authority to act for the processor but never owns the seafood. Coastal Reps is best described as a(n):
questions.explanation: An agent or broker has legal authority to act on behalf of another channel member and does not take title. A wholesaler or distributor buys (takes title to) the goods it resells.

questions.stem: Fraser Valley Supply buys canned goods from processors and resells them in case lots to independent grocery and convenience stores across B.C. Which intermediary term fits best?
questions.explanation: A wholesaler sells to other intermediaries, usually retailers, and the term usually applies to consumer goods. It is not a retailer because it does not sell to consumers, and not an agent or broker because it takes title to the goods.

questions.stem: Prairie Industrial Supply stocks bearings, belts and hydraulic hoses, sells them to farm-equipment repair shops and mining companies, and lets customers pay on 60-day terms. Which term is usually used for this kind of intermediary?
questions.explanation: A distributor performs many functions (selling, maintaining inventory, extending credit), and the term is usually used for business markets. A broker or agent would not hold inventory or take title, and a retailer sells to final consumers.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a distributor from a wholesaler as the terms are used in Figure 10-1?
options: A distributor never takes title to the goods it sells, whereas a wholesaler always takes title
A distributor sells only to final consumers, whereas a wholesaler sells only to manufacturers
Both terms mean an intermediary with legal authority to act on a manufacturer's behalf
'Distributor' usually means a multi-function intermediary in business markets; 'wholesaler' usually means consumer goods
questions.explanation: Figure 10-1: a distributor performs a variety of functions and the term is usually used for business markets, while a wholesaler sells to other intermediaries (usually retailers) and usually refers to consumer goods. Legal authority to act on another's behalf describes an agent or broker.

questions.stem: In Figure 10-1, 'dealer' is a general term that can mean the same as a distributor, a retailer or a wholesaler.
questions.explanation: True. 'Dealer' is the catch-all term in Figure 10-1; 'middleman', the other generic word, simply means an intermediary.

questions.stem: Which statement about marketing intermediary terms is NOT correct?
options: An agent takes title to the goods it sells on a manufacturer's behalf
A wholesaler sells to other intermediaries, usually retailers
questions.explanation: Agents and brokers act on behalf of another channel member but do NOT take title; that is their defining feature. The other statements match Figure 10-1.

questions.stem: As in Figure 10-2, four producers each want to sell to four buyers. How many contacts are needed with no intermediary, and how many when all trade goes through one intermediary?
questions.explanation: No intermediary: producers x buyers = 4 x 4 = 16. One intermediary: producers + buyers = 4 + 4 = 8. Answering 4 with the intermediary counts only one side, and 8 without / 16 with reverses the two formulas.

questions.stem: Six Okanagan wineries each want to sell to five Calgary restaurants. How many contacts are ELIMINATED if all sales go through one wine distributor?
questions.explanation: Without the distributor: 6 x 5 = 30 contacts. With it: 6 + 5 = 11 contacts. Contacts eliminated = 30 - 11 = 19. Choosing 11 confuses the contacts that remain with the contacts saved.

questions.stem: Why does inserting one intermediary between many producers and many buyers reduce the total number of transactions?
options: Each party contacts only the intermediary, so contacts equal producers + buyers rather than producers x buyers
The intermediary takes title to fewer products than the producers did, so fewer sales are recorded
Buyers purchase less often when an intermediary is present, so fewer orders are placed
The intermediary eliminates transporting and storing, so fewer shipments are needed
questions.explanation: The saving comes from the structure of contacts: everyone connects to one hub instead of to each other. Intermediaries do not eliminate logistical functions such as transporting and storing; they perform them.

questions.stem: Rather than ordering parkas only when customers ask, Northwind Outfitters in Yellowknife keeps a deep stock all year so a customer can buy one the moment a cold snap hits. Which utility is Northwind mainly creating?
questions.explanation: Time utility means having the product available WHEN the buyer wants it, here the instant a cold snap hits. Place utility is about WHERE it is available; the stem stresses timing, not location.

questions.stem: A Halifax appliance retailer offers in-store financing so a young couple can take home a $2,400 fridge today and pay over 18 months. Which utility does the financing create, and how does it differ from place utility?
options: Time utility: it delivers the fridge quickly; place utility would be about the credit terms
Form utility: it changes the fridge's features; place utility would be about the payment plan
Possession utility: it eases ownership; place utility would be having the fridge at a convenient location
Place utility: the couple takes the fridge home; possession utility would be about warehousing
questions.explanation: Possession utility is created by making it easier to acquire and own a product, for example through credit. Place utility is having the product where the buyer wants it, which has nothing to do with payment terms.

questions.stem: Which statement about how intermediaries create value is NOT correct?
options: Adding an intermediary always increases the number of transactions in the channel
With one intermediary, contacts equal the number of producers plus the number of buyers
Without an intermediary, contacts equal the number of producers multiplied by the number of buyers
Intermediaries can create time, place, form and possession utility
questions.explanation: Figure 10-2 shows the opposite: one intermediary cuts 4 x 4 = 16 contacts to 4 + 4 = 8. The other statements are the contact formulas and the four utilities.

questions.stem: A supermarket chain buys fruits and vegetables from different sources, transfers them to its stores, and arranges them for its customers. Which of the following functions is the store performing as an intermediary?
questions.explanation: Gathering products from different sources (selection/assorting), moving them (transporting) and arranging them for shoppers are logistical activities. 'Buys' tempts students toward transactional, but the dominant activity described is gathering, moving and arranging the produce; 'informational function' is not one of the three families.

questions.stem: Maple Leaf Hardware Supply buys hammers from six manufacturers, drills from four others and paint from three more, so a contractor can find everything in one catalogue. Which specific activity is it performing?
questions.explanation: Selection (assorting) is putting together a selection of products from several different sources, a logistical activity. Sorting is different: buying large quantities of a product and dividing them into smaller amounts.

questions.stem: A Lethbridge produce wholesaler buys potatoes by the truckload from growers and repacks them into 10-pound bags for small grocers. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Purchasing in large quantities and dividing into smaller amounts is sorting (bulk breaking), which is logistical. Selection would be gathering products from many sources, and neither selection nor storing is transactional.

questions.stem: Northern Plains Distributors lets its rural hardware-store customers pay for spring inventory 90 days after delivery. Which function family does this represent?
questions.explanation: Extending credit to customers is financing, a facilitating function. It is not transactional (buying, selling, risk-taking) even though money is involved.

questions.stem: A Montreal clothing wholesaler buys 20,000 winter jackets in March for next season and will absorb the loss if a warm winter leaves them unsold. Which activity, and which function family, does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Assuming the business risk of owning inventory is risk-taking, a transactional function. Students often file risk under facilitating, but Figure 10-3 places risk-taking with buying and selling because it comes from ownership.

questions.stem: TrueNorth Foods Wholesale sends its suppliers monthly reports on which snack flavours are gaining share in Atlantic Canada and what competitors are discounting. This is:
options: selling and promotion, a transactional function
marketing information and research, a facilitating function
selection and assorting, a logistical function
risk-taking on inventory, a transactional function
questions.explanation: Providing information to customers and suppliers, including competitive conditions and trends, is marketing information and research, a facilitating function. It is not selling, because no products are being promoted and no orders sought.

questions.stem: An electronics distributor's sales reps call on retailers, demonstrate new products and take orders. Which function family is being performed?
questions.explanation: Contacting potential customers, promoting products and seeking orders is selling, a transactional function. Demonstrations share information, but the purpose is to sell; 'informational' is not one of the three families.

questions.stem: Before reselling, a Prairie grain handler inspects each farmer's wheat, tests its protein content and assigns it a quality grade. In Figure 10-3 terms, this is:
questions.explanation: Inspecting, testing and assigning quality grades is grading, listed with the facilitating functions. In channel vocabulary 'sorting' does not mean sorting by quality; it means buying in bulk and dividing into smaller amounts.

questions.stem: A Thunder Bay wholesaler keeps snowblowers in a regional warehouse close to its dealers and runs its own trucks to deliver them when dealers reorder. Both activities belong to which function family?
options: Logistical for storing, but transactional for transporting
questions.explanation: Storing (assembling and protecting products at a convenient location) and transporting (physically moving products to customers) are both logistical functions in Figure 10-3. Transporting is not transactional; transactional covers buying, selling and risk-taking.

questions.stem: Which pair places both activities in the SAME function family?
questions.explanation: Sorting and selection are both logistical. Risk-taking (transactional) and financing (facilitating) is the classic trap pair; buying is transactional while storing is logistical; transporting is logistical while marketing research is facilitating.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a logistical function?
questions.explanation: Risk-taking is transactional because it comes from owning inventory. The logistical functions are selection (assorting), storing, sorting and transporting.

questions.stem: All of the following are transactional functions EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Financing (extending credit to customers) is a facilitating function. The transactional functions are buying, selling and risk-taking.

questions.stem: Purchasing products for resale is called _____, while purchasing in large quantities and dividing them into smaller amounts is called _____.
questions.explanation: Buying (transactional) is purchasing products for resale; sorting (logistical) is buying in large quantities and dividing into smaller amounts. Selection means gathering products from several different sources.

questions.stem: Alder Furniture cuts out its wholesaler and begins selling directly to retailers. What happens to the storing, sorting and financing functions the wholesaler used to perform?
options: They disappear, because no intermediary remains to perform them
They must still be performed, by Alder, by the retailers or by someone else
They become transactional functions once the wholesaler is gone
questions.explanation: You can eliminate an intermediary, but not its functions: products still have to be stored, broken into smaller lots and financed. The work shifts to another channel member, which is why removing a partner only pays if someone else can do the job more efficiently.

questions.stem: Cold Lake Seafoods is choosing a channel partner. It most needs a partner that will extend credit to small restaurant customers and supply data on menu and competitor trends. Which type of functions is it primarily looking for?
questions.explanation: Financing (credit) and marketing information and research are both facilitating functions. Logistical functions (selection, storing, sorting, transporting) handle the physical product, which is not the need described.

questions.stem: When a company uses intermediaries like wholesalers and retailers to distribute its products, it is following which distribution strategy?
questions.explanation: In indirect marketing channels, intermediaries are inserted between the producer and consumers and perform numerous channel functions. 'Online' is not a channel type: online sales can be direct (a brand's own site) or indirect (through Amazon).

questions.stem: Aurora Skincare sells only through its own website and ships every order from its Kelowna facility to the customer's door. No other company resells its products. Which channel is Aurora using?
questions.explanation: A direct channel is one in which the producer and the ultimate consumer deal directly with each other, with no intermediaries. Dual distribution would require two or more types of channels; Aurora uses only one.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts direct and indirect channels?
options: A direct channel is any channel that uses the Internet; an indirect channel uses physical stores
Direct: producer and ultimate consumer deal with each other; indirect: intermediaries are inserted between them
A direct channel always has lower total costs than an indirect channel for the same product
In an indirect channel the producer still performs all of the channel functions itself
questions.explanation: The test is whether intermediaries exist, not the medium used. Direct channels are not automatically cheaper because intermediaries often perform functions more efficiently, and in indirect channels the intermediaries take on many of the functions.

questions.stem: A small Ontario jam maker that sells its jars through Amazon's online store is using a direct channel because the sale happens online.
questions.explanation: False. Corrected statement: the jam maker is using an indirect channel because Amazon is an intermediary between it and the consumer. A channel is direct only when producer and consumer deal with each other with no intermediaries, online or offline.

questions.stem: Peak Analytics makes complex, custom-configured laboratory instruments bought by a small number of hospitals and universities, each needing extensive technical consultation before purchase. Which channel approach fits best?
options: An indirect channel through wholesalers and retailers
Intensive distribution through as many outlets as possible
A long channel with an agent, a wholesaler and a retailer
A direct channel using the company's own technical sales force
questions.explanation: Technical complexity, high unit value and few buyers all point to a short, direct channel where the producer can provide expert information. Long indirect channels suit low-value, standardized products sold to many buyers.

questions.stem: Polar Pops, a small Winnipeg candy maker, wants its chocolate bars in thousands of convenience stores across Canada. According to the chapter, which consumer channel is most common for low-cost, low-unit-value items like this?
questions.explanation: Channel C (producer, wholesaler, retailer, consumer) is the most common for low-cost, low-unit-value items such as candy and magazines: the wholesaler breaks bulk and reaches many small stores economically. Producer -> Retailer -> Consumer works when a large retailer buys directly, which thousands of small convenience stores cannot do.

questions.stem: Canadian Tire buys barbecues directly from the manufacturer in huge volumes and sells them to shoppers in its stores. Which consumer channel structure is this?
questions.explanation: Channel B is used when a large retailer such as Walmart or Canadian Tire buys directly from the producer, so no wholesaler is needed. Channel C adds a wholesaler, typical for low-unit-value items sold through many small retailers.

questions.stem: Sweet Prairie, a large candy maker, uses independent agents who earn commissions for connecting it with regional wholesalers; the wholesalers then supply retailers. Which channel is this, and what role does the agent play?
options: Producer -> Wholesaler -> Retailer -> Consumer; 'agent' is just another name for the wholesaler
Producer -> Agent -> Wholesaler -> Retailer -> Consumer; the agent links producer and wholesalers, without title
Producer -> Retailer -> Consumer; the agent acts as the retailer selling to shoppers
Producer -> Agent -> Consumer; the agent takes title and sells directly to shoppers
questions.explanation: Channel D adds an agent in front of the wholesaler; agents bring producers and wholesalers together (Mars candy is the chapter's example) and, unlike wholesalers, do not take title. An agent is not just another name for a wholesaler.

questions.stem: Which consumer channel example is NOT correctly matched with its structure?
options: Walmart buying from manufacturers: Producer -> Retailer -> Consumer
Dell selling computers on its own website: Producer -> Agent -> Wholesaler -> Retailer -> Consumer
Magazines sold in corner stores: Producer -> Wholesaler -> Retailer -> Consumer
questions.explanation: Dell selling on its own site is the chapter's example of the direct channel A (Producer -> Consumer), not the longest channel D. The other three pairings match the chapter's figure.

questions.stem: In consumer channel D, which member comes immediately after the producer?
