questions.explanation: Channel D runs Producer -> Agent -> Wholesaler -> Retailer -> Consumer, so the agent comes right after the producer. Industrial distributors appear only in business (B2B) channels.

questions.stem: Rockies Heavy Equipment buys loaders and excavators from a manufacturer, holds them in inventory, and sells and services them for construction firms in its region. In a business channel, Rockies is acting as a(n):
questions.explanation: An industrial distributor performs functions similar to a wholesaler in business markets: taking title, holding inventory and reselling to industrial users (the chapter's Caterpillar example). Agents and brokers do not take title or possession, and retailers sell to consumers.

questions.stem: In business channel D (Producer -> Agent -> Industrial distributor -> Industrial user), how do the agent and the industrial distributor differ?
options: The agent takes title and holds the inventory; the industrial distributor only negotiates sales for a commission
Both take title to the goods, but only the agent extends credit to industrial users
The agent arranges sales without taking title or possession; the distributor takes title and holds inventory
The agent sells to final consumers; the industrial distributor sells mainly to retailers
questions.explanation: Agents do not take title or physical possession of goods; they negotiate on the producer's behalf. The industrial distributor, like a wholesaler, buys, stocks and resells to industrial users. Neither sells to consumers in a B2B channel.

questions.stem: Hartland Sensors, a small Ontario maker of industrial sensors, cannot afford its own sales force but wants to reach manufacturing plants across Canada. Sensors ship straight from its factory to each plant. Which business channel fits best?
options: Producer -> Industrial user, using its own sales force
questions.explanation: An agent can represent the producer and negotiate sales without the firm building a sales force, and because goods ship directly from the factory no distributor is needed to hold inventory. The direct option requires the sales force Hartland cannot afford, and the other two are consumer channels.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the business (B2B) channel structures described in the chapter?
questions.explanation: Business channels end with an industrial user, never a consumer, and never include a retailer. The other three are channels A, B and C of the B2B figure.

questions.stem: Why does a company like IBM sell large computing systems to major corporations through a direct channel rather than through distributors?
options: Complex, expensive systems sold to a few large buyers justify a direct sales force with technical expertise
Business law requires producers of all industrial products to sell through direct channels
Industrial distributors are not permitted to stock or resell technology products
Direct channels always cost less than indirect channels, whatever the product or buyer
questions.explanation: Business channels tend to be direct when products are technical and high in unit value and customers are few and large, because the producer's own sales force can supply the information buyers need. Nothing requires direct channels, and direct is not automatically cheaper.

questions.stem: Expedia lets travellers compare and book flights and hotels from many suppliers on its website. Expedia is an example of a(n):
questions.explanation: Electronic marketing channels use the Internet to make goods and services available. Expedia is an intermediary between travellers and the airlines and hotels, so it is not a direct channel from the producers' point of view.

questions.stem: Northern Home Shopping, a TV channel, airs product demonstrations and viewers phone in their orders; no salesperson ever meets the buyer. This is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Direct marketing channels let consumers buy by interacting with advertising media (catalogues, telemarketing, direct mail, TV home shopping, online) without a face-to-face meeting with a salesperson.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a direct marketing channel from a direct channel?
options: Direct marketing is buying via media (catalogue, TV, online) with no salesperson; a direct channel has no intermediaries
They are identical terms for a producer selling straight to consumers with no intermediaries involved
A direct marketing channel always includes a retailer, while a direct channel always includes a wholesaler
A direct channel uses only the Internet, while a direct marketing channel uses only telephone sales
questions.explanation: The terms answer different questions: direct marketing is HOW the buyer purchases (through media, no salesperson); a direct channel is about WHO is in the channel (no intermediaries). A TV shopping network that sells many brands is a direct marketing channel but is still an intermediary.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the e-commerce trends highlighted in the course?
options: Using AI for personalization, along with AR and VR
Moving away from free delivery to cut costs
Offering multiple payment options such as buy now, pay later
questions.explanation: The trends slide lists fast, free delivery as a trend, the opposite of dropping it. AI, AR and VR, multiple payment options, social selling and voice activation are all on the list, along with CRM, hybrid commerce, data privacy and sustainability.

questions.stem: According to the course's e-commerce trends slide, which two product categories lead online sales?
questions.explanation: The slide names fashion and electronics as the top e-commerce categories. The other pairs are plausible guesses but are not the categories the course identifies.

questions.stem: A firm that reaches buyers by using two or more different types of channels for the same basic product is using:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of dual distribution. A strategic channel alliance uses another firm's channel, and intensive distribution is about how many outlets carry the product, not how many channel types.

questions.stem: Prairie Peak Outerwear sells the same parkas through Sport Chek stores and through its own online store. Which channel arrangement is this?
questions.explanation: One firm, one basic product, two different channel types (an indirect retail channel and its own direct online channel) = dual distribution. It is not a strategic channel alliance, because Prairie Peak is not using another producer's distribution network.

questions.stem: Which scenario is dual distribution rather than a strategic channel alliance?
options: A small tea brand's products ride on a large cookie maker's delivery trucks to the cookie maker's grocery accounts
A regional airline's flights are sold through a larger airline's booking system
A cereal maker sells its granola through grocery chains and through its own subscription website
A snack brand uses a soft-drink company's vending-machine network to reach consumers
questions.explanation: Dual distribution is one firm using two or more of its own channel types for the same product. In the other three, one firm's marketing channel is used to sell another firm's products, which is the definition of a strategic channel alliance.

questions.stem: What is a common risk of dual distribution?
options: Losing the ability to reach more than one market segment
Being forced to give up ownership of the product
Eliminating the need for any intermediary functions
Channel conflict, since the channels may compete for the same customers
questions.explanation: Using two channel types for the same product can pit them against each other, for example a retailer resenting the maker's own online store, which is a source of channel conflict. Dual distribution is used precisely to reach more segments, not fewer.

questions.stem: When a firm uses dual distribution, its website can play multiple roles, such as taking orders (a transactional role) and providing product information (a promotional role).
questions.explanation: True. The chapter notes that websites can play multiple roles, transactional and promotional, when a firm uses them alongside its other channels.

questions.stem: An arrangement whereby one firm's marketing channel is used to sell another firm's products is called a:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of a strategic channel alliance (e.g., Starbucks coffee sold in Safeway). Dual distribution involves one firm using two or more of its own channel types.

questions.stem: Nordic Chips, a Quebec snack maker, signs an agreement under which a national soft-drink company sells Nordic's chips through the soft-drink company's own vending-machine route network. This is a:
questions.explanation: One firm's marketing channel (the soft-drink company's vending routes) is used to sell another firm's products. It is not disintermediation, because no channel member is being bypassed.

questions.stem: Which scenario is best classified as a strategic channel alliance?
options: A paint maker sells the same paint through national hardware chains and through its own online store
A B.C. kombucha maker's drinks ride on a national juice company's trucks and sales force to the juice company's stores
Two unrelated bakeries in Moncton share the cost of one delivery van and a joint market booth
A tire maker opens its own chain of tire and service centres in major cities across Canada
questions.explanation: In an alliance, one firm's channel sells another firm's products. The paint maker is dual distribution, the bakeries pooling resources at the same level form a horizontal marketing system, and the tire maker owning outlets is forward integration.

questions.stem: Why might a small brand enter a strategic channel alliance with a larger company?
options: It gains legal ownership of the partner's retail stores and warehouses
It is guaranteed exclusive distribution in every market it enters
It eliminates all possibility of channel conflict with retailers
It gains established distribution that would be costly or slow to build itself
questions.explanation: Using another firm's channel lets the smaller brand reach buyers quickly without building its own sales force and delivery network. Owning the partner's outlets would be integration (a corporate VMS), which an alliance does not involve.

questions.stem: In a strategic channel alliance, the firm whose products are being sold must own the partner's distribution channel.
questions.explanation: False. Corrected statement: in a strategic channel alliance one firm's marketing channel is used to sell another firm's products, with no ownership required. Owning successive channel stages would be a corporate VMS.

questions.stem: Omni-channel retailing is:
options: the concept of a seamless shopping experience among all shopping channels.
a historical term describing retailing before technology revolutionized the shopping process.
when a retailer closes either its online or offline marketing channel to focus on the remaining channel.
questions.explanation: Omni-channel retailing creates a seamless experience among all available shopping channels: online, catalogue and in-store. It is not just another word for multichannel marketing, which blends channels so they reinforce each other; omni-channel goes further by making them feel like one experience.

questions.stem: Huron Home, a home decor retailer, lets shoppers start a cart in its app, check live in-store stock, pick up at any store, return online orders in store and earn the same loyalty points everywhere, all as one continuous experience. This best illustrates:
questions.explanation: A single, seamless experience across every shopping channel is omni-channel retailing. Dual distribution only requires two channel types for the same product; it says nothing about integrating them into one experience.

questions.stem: Which scenario reflects multichannel marketing but NOT yet omni-channel retailing?
options: A retailer's catalogue drives web visits and its website drives store traffic, but carts and returns stay separate by channel
A retailer's app, website and stores share one cart, one loyalty account and one live inventory system
A retailer closes all of its physical stores to focus only on selling through its website
A manufacturer sells its products through one exclusive dealer per city across the country
questions.explanation: Multichannel marketing blends communication and delivery channels so they reinforce each other; omni-channel requires the customer to experience them seamlessly. Separate carts and returns mean the channels support each other but are not yet seamless.

questions.stem: Maya tries on running shoes at a Toronto store, then orders them later on her phone. In multichannel terms, the store visit took place in the _____ and the phone order in the _____.
questions.explanation: The marketplace is the traditional face-to-face environment; the marketspace is the online, face-to-screen environment. Reversing them is the usual mistake: think of 'space' as in cyberspace.

questions.stem: Why do firms practise multichannel marketing?
options: To make each channel fully independent so that the channels compete for the same customers
To avoid all face-to-face contact with consumers by moving every sale to the marketspace
To cut the number of channels down to the single channel that is most profitable
To leverage each channel's strengths so the channels reinforce one another in building relationships
questions.explanation: Multichannel marketing blends communication and delivery channels that are mutually reinforcing, leveraging what each does best. Letting channels compete for the same customers is the conflict that multichannel marketing tries to avoid.

questions.stem: In the global channel of distribution (Figure 10-7), what comes immediately after the seller's international marketing headquarters?
questions.explanation: The sequence is Seller -> Seller's international marketing headquarters -> Channels between nations -> Channels within foreign nations -> Final consumer. The product must cross borders before it can be distributed inside the foreign market.

questions.stem: Which link in the global channel of distribution comes immediately before the final consumer?
questions.explanation: Channels within foreign nations (local wholesalers and retailers) deliver the product to the final consumer. Channels between nations come earlier, moving the product from the home country into the foreign market.

questions.stem: According to the chapter, channel sophistication in a foreign market tends to increase as:
options: the distance from the seller's home country increases
the seller opens more international headquarters
the number of competing sellers declines
questions.explanation: The chapter states that channel sophistication increases as a country's economic infrastructure develops, since developed economies have more specialized intermediaries. Distance and number of competitors are not the stated driver.

questions.stem: Banff Botanicals ships its skincare products to a freight forwarder and export agent who move them from Canada into Japan. These firms belong to which link of the global channel?
questions.explanation: Firms that move products from the home country to the foreign country form the channels between nations. Channels within foreign nations handle distribution once the product is inside Japan.

questions.stem: Once Banff Botanicals' products reach Japan, a Tokyo wholesaler supplies them to department stores across the country. How does this wholesaler's role differ from the export agent's?
options: The Tokyo wholesaler is part of channels within foreign nations; the export agent was part of channels between nations
Both are part of channels between nations, since both handle imported goods
The Tokyo wholesaler is the seller's international marketing headquarters
The export agent is part of channels within foreign nations; the wholesaler is between nations
questions.explanation: Distribution inside the foreign market (wholesaler to department stores) is channels within foreign nations; moving goods across the border is channels between nations. The international marketing headquarters belongs to the seller, not to a foreign intermediary.

questions.stem: Professionally managed and centrally coordinated marketing channels designed to achieve channel economies and maximum marketing impact are called:
questions.explanation: This is the definition of a vertical marketing system (VMS). A horizontal marketing system links firms at the same level instead of centrally coordinating the levels of a channel.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a vertical marketing system and a horizontal marketing system?
options: A VMS always involves franchising; a horizontal system always involves ownership
A VMS is used only in business markets; a horizontal system only in consumer markets
A VMS links competitors at the same level; a horizontal system links suppliers and retailers
A VMS coordinates different channel levels; a horizontal system pools unrelated firms at the same level
questions.explanation: 'Vertical' means up and down the channel (producer, wholesaler, retailer); 'horizontal' means side by side at the same level. Franchising is only one form of contractual VMS, so 'always franchising' is wrong.

questions.stem: Two unrelated Moncton businesses, a craft brewery and an artisan cheese maker, share the cost of a refrigerated delivery van and a joint booth at farmers' markets. This is best described as a:
questions.explanation: Two or more unrelated companies at the same channel level (both are producers) pooling resources form a horizontal marketing system. A VMS would coordinate different levels, and a retailer-sponsored cooperative is formed by retailers, not producers.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the three types of vertical marketing systems?
questions.explanation: The three VMS types are corporate (ownership), contractual (contracts) and administered (size and influence). A horizontal marketing system is the contrasting idea of firms at the same level pooling resources.

questions.stem: Why do channel members form a vertical marketing system instead of operating as independent firms?
options: Central coordination achieves channel economies and maximum marketing impact
So each member can maximize its own profit regardless of the others
To eliminate the need for logistics activities
To bring unrelated firms at the same level together to share resources
questions.explanation: A VMS is professionally managed and centrally coordinated precisely to gain channel economies and marketing impact. Independent members chasing their own profit describes the conventional channel a VMS replaces; pooling at the same level is horizontal.

questions.stem: Mocha Jive coffee shops operate their own cafés and have a subsidiary company, Perfect Cookies, that produces a wide variety of cookies and snacks for their stores. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: A retailer owning the manufacturing operation that supplies it is backward integration, which creates a corporate VMS. It is not a horizontal marketing system, which would require unrelated firms at the same level pooling resources.

questions.stem: Laurentian Leather, a Quebec handbag maker, buys a chain of 30 boutiques so that it controls how its bags are displayed and sold. This is:
questions.explanation: A producer acquiring intermediaries downstream (closer to the consumer) is forward integration, creating a corporate VMS. Backward integration runs the other way: a retailer or wholesaler acquiring production.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes forward from backward integration?
options: Forward: a producer owns intermediaries closer to the consumer; backward: a retailer or wholesaler owns production
Forward: a retailer owns the manufacturer that supplies it; backward: a manufacturer opens its own stores
Forward integration relies on contracts between firms, while backward integration relies on ownership
Both terms describe two firms at the same channel level merging to pool their resources
questions.explanation: Direction is measured from the firm doing the acquiring: toward the consumer = forward, toward the source = backward. Both involve ownership (corporate VMS); the reversed definitions are the classic trap.

questions.stem: A corporate vertical marketing system is characterized by:
options: contracts among independently owned firms at different levels
coordination through the size and influence of one dominant member
unrelated firms at the same level pooling resources
ownership of successive stages of production and distribution by one firm
questions.explanation: Corporate VMS = ownership, achieved through forward or backward integration. Contracts describe a contractual VMS; size and influence describe an administered VMS.

questions.stem: Harvest Moon Grocers, a Saskatchewan supermarket chain, is frustrated by inconsistent supply of its private-label bread and wants permanent control over production. Which move would create a corporate VMS through backward integration?
options: Signing a franchise agreement with a national bakery brand
Joining a retailer-sponsored cooperative with other grocers
Buying the bakery that produces its private-label bread
Letting the largest bread brand manage its shelf displays
questions.explanation: Owning the upstream supplier is backward integration, which creates a corporate VMS. A franchise agreement or cooperative would be contractual, and letting a dominant brand manage the shelves would be an administered arrangement.

questions.stem: Which is NOT an example of a corporate VMS?
options: Apple selling its products through its own Apple Stores
An independent hardware store joining Home Hardware's retailer-owned cooperative
Ralph Lauren operating its own chain of Polo stores
A coffee chain owning the bakery that makes its cookies
questions.explanation: A retailer-sponsored cooperative is a contractual VMS: the stores stay independently owned and coordinate by agreement. The other three involve one firm owning successive stages (forward or backward integration).

questions.stem: Valley Fresh, a Nova Scotia food wholesaler, signs up 60 independently owned grocers who agree to buy through Valley Fresh, use a common store banner and follow its merchandising program. This is a:
questions.explanation: A wholesaler that contracts with independent retailers to standardize and coordinate buying and merchandising sponsors a voluntary chain (IGA is the chapter's example). If the retailers had banded together to own the wholesale operation, it would be a cooperative.

questions.stem: Two hundred independent hardware store owners jointly own and operate a wholesale buying organization that supplies all their stores under a shared banner. This is a:
questions.explanation: Independent retailers banding together to run their own wholesale operation form a retailer-sponsored cooperative (Home Hardware is the chapter's example). It is a contractual VMS, not corporate, because each store remains independently owned. Although all the owners are retailers, they jointly run the wholesale stage that supplies them, so this is a vertical (contractual) arrangement, not a horizontal marketing system of unrelated firms.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a wholesaler-sponsored voluntary chain and a retailer-sponsored cooperative?
options: The sponsor: a wholesaler organizes a voluntary chain, while independent retailers organize a cooperative
A voluntary chain is coordinated through ownership, while a cooperative is coordinated through influence
A voluntary chain charges franchise fees, while a cooperative operates with no agreements at all
There is no real difference, since both are examples of an administered VMS
questions.explanation: Both are contractual VMSs; the difference is the sponsor. Wholesaler-sponsored = IGA-style voluntary chain; retailer-sponsored = Home Hardware-style cooperative. Neither is based on ownership or on mere influence.

questions.stem: Coca-Cola licenses independent bottlers in each territory, who buy syrup, bottle the drink and sell it to retailers. This is an example of a:
questions.explanation: The bottlers are franchised wholesalers (they sell to retailers) under a manufacturer's sponsorship. A manufacturer-sponsored RETAIL franchise, like Ford dealers, licenses outlets that sell to final consumers.

questions.stem: Kodiak Motors authorizes independently owned dealerships across Canada to sell and service its vehicles under the Kodiak brand. This is a:
questions.explanation: A manufacturer licensing independent retailers (dealers) to sell its product to consumers is a manufacturer-sponsored retail franchise system, like Ford dealers. It is not forward integration, because Kodiak does not own the dealerships.

questions.stem: Which example is NOT correctly matched with its contractual VMS type?
options: Ford dealers: manufacturer-sponsored retail franchise system
questions.explanation: Coca-Cola bottlers are a manufacturer-sponsored wholesale franchise system. Service-sponsored franchise systems are illustrated by firms such as Holiday Inn and McDonald's.

questions.stem: In the chapter's classification of franchise programs, McDonald's and Holiday Inn are examples of a:
questions.explanation: McDonald's and Holiday Inn are the chapter's examples of service-sponsored franchise systems, in which a service company licenses franchisees to operate under its name. They do not manufacture a product for dealers or bottlers to resell.

questions.stem: In an administered vertical marketing system, coordination among successive stages is achieved through:
options: the size and influence of one channel member
ownership of the stages by one firm
a wholesale operation owned by retailers
questions.explanation: Administered VMS = coordination through one member's size and influence (e.g., Procter & Gamble), with no ownership and no binding contracts. Ownership is corporate; franchise contracts and retailer-owned wholesalers are contractual.

questions.stem: Because its brands are must-haves for grocers, Brightway, a giant household products maker, gets independent supermarket chains to follow its shelf-layout plans and promotion calendars, even though it owns no stores and has no franchise contracts with them. This is a(n):
questions.explanation: Coordination that comes from a dominant member's size and influence, without ownership or contracts, is an administered VMS. Corporate would require ownership of the stores; contractual would require formal agreements such as franchises.

questions.stem: A national retailer dictates package sizes, delivery schedules and pricing terms to hundreds of independent suppliers simply because of its enormous purchase volumes. It owns none of them and has no franchise or cooperative agreements with them. Why is this an administered rather than a corporate or contractual VMS?
options: The retailer owns the successive stages of production and distribution
The suppliers have signed franchise agreements with the retailer
The suppliers and the retailer are at the same channel level
Coordination comes from the retailer's size and influence, not ownership or contracts
questions.explanation: Administered VMSs rely on size and power (Walmart and P&G are the classic examples). Ownership would make it corporate and franchise or cooperative agreements would make it contractual; suppliers and retailer are at different levels, so it is vertical, not horizontal.

questions.stem: Which situation is NOT an example of an administered VMS?
options: A grocery chain buys the dairy that supplies its private-label milk
Procter & Gamble's influence leads retailers to cooperate on displays and promotions
Walmart's buying power leads suppliers to adopt its inventory systems
A dominant toy maker persuades independent stores to follow its merchandising guidelines
questions.explanation: Buying the supplier is ownership, which is backward integration in a corporate VMS. The other three achieve coordination through size and influence alone, the mark of an administered VMS.

questions.stem: Brandt Appliances, the market-leading appliance maker, wants independent dealers to adopt its display standards and sales training, but it does not want to buy stores or sign franchise contracts. What approach is it relying on?
options: An administered VMS, using its size and influence to secure cooperation
A horizontal marketing system with competing appliance makers
questions.explanation: Without ownership (corporate) or contracts (contractual), Brandt's only coordinating mechanism is its market power, which makes this an administered VMS. Owning dealers would in any case be forward, not backward, integration.

questions.stem: Fresh Catch, a Nova Scotia exporter of live lobster, uses the shortest possible channel so its lobsters reach restaurants alive, before they can die and spoil. Which factor most directly drives this choice?
options: Desire for channel control, a company factor
questions.explanation: Perishable products need short or direct channels so they reach buyers before they spoil. Unit value is also a product factor, but the stem's cue is that the product is live and spoils quickly.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a product factor affecting channel choice?
questions.explanation: Geographic concentration of buyers is a market factor. The product factors are technical factors, perishability, unit value and product life cycle stage.

questions.stem: Which pairing of channel-choice factor and factor group is correct?
options: Desire for channel control: product factor
Number of potential customers: product factor
questions.explanation: Market factors are geographic concentration, number of potential customers, type of market and order size. Perishability is a product factor, desire for channel control is a company factor, and number of potential customers is a market factor.

questions.stem: Snackwise sells low-priced granola bars bought in small quantities by millions of consumers across Canada. Based on market and product factors, which channel is most appropriate?
options: A longer, indirect channel using wholesalers and retailers
A direct channel with its own sales force calling on each consumer
Exclusive distribution through one retailer per province
A short direct channel justified by high unit value
questions.explanation: Many dispersed customers, small order sizes and low unit value all point to a longer, indirect channel in which intermediaries spread the cost of reaching buyers. High unit value is the opposite of this product.

questions.stem: Why does low unit value generally push a producer toward a longer, indirect channel?
options: Low-value products are always perishable, so they must pass through many intermediaries
Intermediaries refuse to carry high-value products, so only low-value ones are left for them
Each sale is too small to pay for direct contact, so intermediaries spread costs over many products
Low-value products are always technically complex and need many specialists to sell them
questions.explanation: With low unit value, the margin on each sale cannot cover the cost of direct contact, while intermediaries carrying many products can reach buyers more cheaply. Technical complexity points the other way, toward direct channels.

questions.stem: Bytewise, a young Ottawa start-up with limited cash and little distribution experience, relies on established distributors instead of building its own warehouses and sales force. Which group of channel factors is driving this?
options: Company factors: financial resources and ability of management
Market factors: geographic concentration of buyers
Product factors: perishability of the goods
Market factors: type of market served
questions.explanation: A firm's own financial resources and management ability are company factors, and limited resources push it toward intermediaries. Nothing in the stem concerns where customers are or how perishable the product is.

questions.stem: Which of the following channel designs are chosen for specialty products or services like high-end sports vehicles, exclusive women's jewellery, and yachts because only one retail outlet in a specified geographical area carries these products?
questions.explanation: Exclusive distribution means only one retailer in a specified geographic area carries the product, and it is typically chosen for specialty products such as specialty automobiles, some fragrances and yachts. Selective distribution uses a few retailers per area (shopping goods); dual distribution is about channel types, not coverage.

questions.stem: Which product category is MOST likely to use exclusive distribution?
questions.explanation: Exclusive distribution suits specialty products, which buyers will make a special effort to find (luxury cars, yachts, high-end fragrances). Convenience products are the opposite: they need intensive distribution in as many outlets as possible.

questions.stem: Fizzi, a Canadian sparkling water brand, wants its cans in every grocery store, gas station, vending machine and convenience store in the country. This coverage strategy is:
questions.explanation: Placing a product in as many outlets as possible is intensive distribution, typical for convenience goods. Dual distribution concerns using two or more channel types, not the number of outlets.

questions.stem: Whirlwind, a mid-priced appliance brand, is carried by only a few retailers in each city, for example three stores in Edmonton, so shoppers can compare models while dealers earn enough to provide good service. This is:
questions.explanation: Using a few retailers in a specific geographic area is selective distribution, typical for shopping goods such as appliances and apparel. Exclusive distribution would mean only one retailer in Edmonton.

questions.stem: Which pairing of target market coverage strategy and product type is correct?
options: Intensive distribution: specialty goods such as yachts
Selective distribution: shopping goods such as appliances and apparel
Exclusive distribution: convenience goods such as gum
Selective distribution: convenience goods such as batteries
questions.explanation: The course mapping is convenience -> intensive, shopping -> selective, specialty -> exclusive. The wrong options swap the extremes, which is the most common trap.

questions.stem: Why would a luxury fragrance maker choose exclusive rather than intensive distribution?
options: Few outlets protect the brand's prestige and dealer service, and buyers will seek the brand out
Exclusive distribution maximizes the number of outlets and encourages impulse purchases
Exclusive distribution guarantees consumers the lowest possible retail price for the fragrance
Intensive distribution is not permitted for premium consumer products such as fragrances
questions.explanation: Specialty goods are bought by customers willing to make a special effort, so one outlet per area is enough and protects image and dealer service. Maximizing outlets and impulse purchases describes intensive distribution for convenience goods.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the target market coverage options considered in channel design?
questions.explanation: Target market coverage is intensive, selective or exclusive. Dual distribution is a different decision (two or more channel types for the same product) and appears as a distractor in the official question.

questions.stem: According to the chapter, which buyer requirements should a channel be designed to satisfy?
options: Sales, inventory levels and treatment of damaged goods
Information, convenience, variety, and pre- and/or post-sale services
questions.explanation: Satisfying buyer requirements means providing information, convenience, variety and pre- and/or post-sale services. Cost, time, capability and dependability are transportation criteria; sales and inventory levels are criteria for evaluating channel members.

questions.stem: TechNest, a Winnipeg electronics retailer, stocks 40 brands of headphones at every price point so shoppers can compare a wide assortment of models. Which buyer requirement is it addressing?
questions.explanation: Variety refers to the breadth and depth of products available, here 40 brands across price points. Convenience would be about ease of access (location, hours, online ordering), not assortment.

questions.stem: Glow Spas, a Calgary hot-tub dealer, delivers and installs every tub it sells and offers a five-year maintenance plan. Which buyer requirement does this address?
questions.explanation: Delivery, installation and ongoing maintenance are pre- and post-sale services. Information would involve explaining the product to buyers before they purchase.

questions.stem: Prairie Pantry extends its store hours to 24/7 and adds curbside pickup so busy parents can shop whenever and however suits them. Which buyer requirement is it improving?
questions.explanation: Convenience covers ease of access: locations, hours, parking and pickup options. Variety would involve expanding the assortment, which the stem does not mention.

questions.stem: A home-security company's new dealer channel delights customers with expert advice and installation, but the dealers' distribution, advertising and selling expenses exceed what they earn on each sale. Which channel design consideration is failing?
questions.explanation: Buyer requirements are being met (advice and installation), but profitability, meaning distribution, advertising and selling expenses relative to revenue, is not. A channel that satisfies buyers but loses money for its members will not last.

questions.stem: Sun Valley Solar sells complex rooftop solar systems to homeowners who are unfamiliar with the technology and need detailed explanations before buying. Which buyer requirement should its channel design emphasize most?
options: Variety: carrying many unrelated product lines
Convenience: stocking panels in convenience stores
Intensive coverage: as many outlets as possible
Information: knowledgeable salespeople who can explain the product
questions.explanation: Buyers of technical, unfamiliar products most need information from knowledgeable salespeople. Intensive coverage and convenience-store placement suit simple convenience goods, not complex systems.

questions.stem: Titan Tools tells a Calgary hardware chain it will stop supplying its best-selling drills unless the chain gives Titan more shelf space. Which source of channel power is Titan using?
questions.explanation: Coercive power rests on the threat of punishment or withdrawal of support. Reward power would offer an incentive for cooperating rather than threatening a penalty.

questions.stem: Crispy Crunch Snacks pays retailers a $2 bonus for every case sold above target and funds their in-store displays. Which source of channel power is it using?
questions.explanation: Reward power uses incentives such as bonuses, allowances and display funding to gain cooperation. Coercive power would threaten a penalty instead.

questions.stem: Boutiques across Canada compete to carry LuxeNord parkas because being associated with the prestigious brand enhances their own image. LuxeNord's influence over these retailers is mainly:
questions.explanation: Referent power exists when other members want to be identified with a respected or admired channel member. Expert power would come from specialized knowledge, which is not why these boutiques cooperate.

questions.stem: Resellers of DataForge's enterprise software follow its recommendations closely because DataForge has unmatched technical knowledge of how to configure the system. Which power source is this?
questions.explanation: Expert power comes from specialized knowledge that others value. Referent power is about wanting to be associated with an admired brand, not about relying on its know-how.

questions.stem: A franchisee that follows head office's pricing rules because its signed franchise agreement gives head office that authority is responding to _____ power, whereas a boutique that cooperates because it admires a designer's brand is responding to _____ power.
questions.explanation: Legitimate power is authority that comes from position or contract (the franchise agreement). Referent power is the desire to be identified with an admired member. Coercive power would require a threat, which neither case involves.

questions.stem: A channel member that coordinates, directs and supports other channel members is called a(n):
questions.explanation: That is the definition of a channel captain, which can be a producer, wholesaler or retailer. 'Middleman' is just another name for any intermediary.

questions.stem: Which statement about the channel captain is NOT correct?
options: It coordinates, directs and supports other channel members
It must always be the manufacturer of the product
It can be a producer, a wholesaler or a retailer
Walmart is an example of a retailer acting as a channel captain
questions.explanation: The channel captain can be any member with the power to lead: producer, wholesaler or retailer (Walmart is the classic retailer example). Assuming it must be the manufacturer is the trap.

questions.stem: Northern Lights Cosmetics is reviewing its retail partners at year-end. Which set of criteria matches the chapter's guidance for evaluating channel members?
options: Cost, time, capability, dependability, accessibility and frequency of each partner's deliveries
Geographic concentration, number of customers, type of market and the partner's order size
Sales, inventory levels, treatment of damaged or lost goods, customer service and promotional cooperation
Information, convenience, variety and pre- and post-sale services offered to buyers
questions.explanation: Channel members are evaluated on sales, inventory levels, treatment of damaged or lost goods, and other factors like customer service and cooperation in promotion. The distractors are the transportation criteria, the market factors and the buyer requirements.

questions.stem: _____ arises when one channel member believes another channel member is engaged in behaviour that prevents it from achieving its goals.
questions.explanation: This is the definition of channel conflict. Disintermediation is one specific cause of conflict (bypassing a member), not the general term.

questions.stem: Tez, an energy drink brand, has a disagreement with one of the major wholesalers of its products over the price of its drinks. What kind of conflict is reflected in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Vertical conflict occurs between different levels of a marketing channel, here a producer and its wholesaler. It is not disintermediation, because Tez is not bypassing the wholesaler, and not horizontal conflict, which would be between two wholesalers.

questions.stem: Two Edmonton dealerships that both sell Kodiak trucks accuse each other of advertising in each other's territory and undercutting prices. This is:
questions.explanation: Horizontal conflict occurs between intermediaries at the same level of the channel, such as two dealers of the same brand. Vertical conflict would be between Kodiak and one of its dealers.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts vertical and horizontal channel conflict?
options: Vertical conflict occurs between different levels of a channel; horizontal conflict occurs between intermediaries at the same level
Vertical conflict occurs between competitors; horizontal conflict occurs between a manufacturer and its retailers
Vertical conflict happens only online; horizontal conflict happens only in stores
Vertical conflict involves only agents; horizontal conflict involves only wholesalers
questions.explanation: Vertical = up and down the channel (e.g., manufacturer vs wholesaler or retailer); horizontal = side by side (e.g., two retailers of the same brand). Saying vertical conflict is between competitors and horizontal conflict is between a manufacturer and its retailers reverses the two definitions.

questions.stem: Kodiak's head office learns that two of its Halifax dealers are fighting over customers because their sales territories overlap. Which action best addresses this horizontal conflict?
options: Bypassing both dealers to sell only through its own website
Clearly defining and enforcing each dealer's sales territory
Raising the wholesale price to both dealers
Adding a third dealer in the same overlapping area
questions.explanation: The conflict is between members at the same level over territory, so clarifying territories removes its cause. Bypassing the dealers would create vertical conflict (disintermediation), and adding another dealer would intensify the overlap.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of vertical conflict?
options: A manufacturer and its wholesaler disagree over price
A manufacturer bypasses its retailers to sell directly to consumers
Two retailers of the same brand fight over the same territory
A manufacturer squeezes its retailers' margins
questions.explanation: Two retailers at the same level is horizontal conflict. The others pit members at different levels against each other; bypassing retailers is disintermediation, a form of vertical conflict.

questions.stem: Lakeshore Mattress has always sold through furniture retailers. It now launches a website that ships mattresses straight to consumers at lower prices, and its retailers protest. What is the specific term for what Lakeshore is doing?
questions.explanation: Disintermediation occurs when a channel member bypasses another member and sells or buys directly, which is what Lakeshore does by selling around its retailers. It is not backward integration, which would mean Lakeshore acquiring an upstream supplier such as a foam maker; disintermediation involves no ownership.

questions.stem: Channel conflict that arises when a channel member bypasses another member and sells or buys products directly from others is called:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of disintermediation. Backward integration involves owning an upstream supplier, not simply bypassing an intermediary.

questions.stem: Disintermediation is best classified as a form of:
options: horizontal conflict, because it involves intermediaries at the same level
strategic channel alliance, because firms share a channel
administered VMS, because one member dominates the others
vertical conflict, because it involves members at different levels when one bypasses another
questions.explanation: When a producer bypasses its retailers (or a buyer bypasses its distributor), the conflict is between different channel levels, so disintermediation is a type of vertical conflict.

questions.stem: Urban Plate, a large Toronto restaurant group, stops buying produce through its foodservice distributor and begins buying directly from Ontario farms. It does not own any farms. The distributor is upset. This is:
questions.explanation: Disintermediation covers bypassing a member to BUY directly as well as to sell directly. It is not backward integration, because Urban Plate is buying from the farms, not owning them.

questions.stem: Which statement about disintermediation is NOT correct?
options: It can occur when a manufacturer sells directly online, bypassing retailers
It can create conflict with the intermediary that is bypassed
It can occur on the buying side, when a buyer bypasses its distributor
It eliminates the channel functions the bypassed intermediary used to perform
questions.explanation: Bypassing an intermediary removes the member, not the functions: storing, transporting, selling and financing must still be done by someone. The other statements are accurate.

questions.stem: Activities that focus on getting the right amount of the right products to the right place at the right time at the lowest possible cost are called:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of logistics. Supply chain management is broader: it integrates information AND logistics activities across all firms in the chain.

questions.stem: How does logistics differ from supply chain management?
options: Logistics covers raw-material suppliers, while SCM covers only activities inside the producer's own warehouse
Logistics is mainly about promotion decisions, while SCM is mainly about pricing decisions in the channel
Logistics manages the flow of goods at lowest cost; SCM integrates information and logistics across all firms in the chain
The two terms are interchangeable, since both describe moving goods from producers to consumers
questions.explanation: Logistics is the movement-of-goods piece; SCM integrates information and logistics across suppliers, the producer and the marketing channel. Assigning raw-material suppliers to logistics while confining SCM to one warehouse reverses their scope: SCM is the broader, cross-firm concept.

questions.stem: Boreal Books switches its shipping from rail to air. Transportation costs rise by $40,000 a year, but faster delivery lets it cut inventory costs by $55,000 and stockout costs by $10,000. What is the change in total logistics cost?
questions.explanation: Change in total logistics cost = +$40,000 - $55,000 - $10,000 = -$25,000. Looking only at transportation (+$40,000) ignores the trade-offs, and -$65,000 forgets to offset the higher transportation cost.

questions.stem: Why do logistics managers focus on TOTAL logistics cost rather than minimizing each cost separately?
options: Total cost is always lowest when each separate cost is minimized on its own
Customer service levels have no effect on any of the logistics costs
Costs trade off: cheaper, slower transport can raise inventory and stockout costs
Only transportation costs matter when evaluating logistics decisions
questions.explanation: Total logistics cost covers transportation, materials handling and warehousing, inventory, stockouts, order processing and return goods handling, and these move against each other. Minimizing one in isolation often raises the total.

questions.stem: Cascade Office Supply promises that orders placed by 2 p.m. arrive the next business day, and it keeps that promise on 99% of orders. The 99% figure measures which customer service factor?
questions.explanation: Dependability is the consistency of service, meaning delivering as promised. Time (order cycle or lead time) is the next-day promise itself; the 99% describes how reliably that promise is met.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a component of total logistics cost?
questions.explanation: Total logistics cost includes transportation, materials handling and warehousing, inventory, stockouts, order processing and return goods handling. Advertising is a promotion cost, not a logistics cost.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the four key logistics functions in a supply chain shown in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The four key logistics functions are transportation, order processing, inventory management and warehousing. Market segmentation is a targeting decision, not a logistics function.

questions.stem: The integration and organization of information and logistics activities across firms in a supply chain, for the purpose of creating and delivering goods and services that provide value to consumers, is:
questions.explanation: This is the definition of supply chain management. Logistics alone is the narrower activity of getting the right products to the right place at the right time at the lowest cost.

questions.stem: For a car manufacturer, the steel mills and parts makers that supply it belong to the _____, while the dealers that sell its cars belong to the _____ (Figure 10-9).
questions.explanation: Figure 10-9: the supplier network is all parties supplying raw materials and parts; the marketing channel is all parties distributing and promoting the product. Together they make up the supply chain.

questions.stem: Which statement about the supply chain and the marketing channel is correct?
options: The marketing channel is broader: it includes the supply chain plus promotion
The supply chain includes only raw-material suppliers, not distributors
The supply chain is broader: it includes the supplier network as well as the marketing channel
questions.explanation: A supply chain runs from suppliers through the producer to consumers, so it contains the marketing channel as its downstream part. The marketing channel does not include upstream suppliers.

questions.stem: The chapter says a firm must harmonize its supply chain with its marketing strategy. What does this mean in practice?
options: Always minimize supply chain cost, whatever the firm's chosen marketing strategy
Change the marketing strategy to fit whatever supply chain the firm already has
Design the supply chain to deliver what the target market values, such as speed or low cost
Leave all supply chain decisions to suppliers so marketing can focus on promotion
questions.explanation: Supply chain management exists to create and deliver value to consumers, so its design must support the chosen marketing strategy. Always minimizing cost could undercut a strategy built on fast, reliable service.

questions.stem: Glacier Bikes sets up shared demand forecasts, real-time inventory data and coordinated production schedules with its tire and frame suppliers, its own plants and the retailers that sell its bikes. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Integrating information and logistics activities across suppliers, the producer and channel members is supply chain management. Multichannel marketing concerns blending communication and delivery channels toward consumers, not coordinating suppliers.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the criteria used to evaluate transportation alternatives?
questions.explanation: The six transportation criteria are cost, time, capability, dependability, accessibility and frequency. Perishability is a product factor affecting channel choice, not a transportation criterion.

questions.stem: Polar Pharma must move vaccines that need to stay at -20 C, so it only considers carriers with refrigerated equipment. Which transportation criterion is it focusing on?
questions.explanation: Capability is the ability of a mode or carrier to provide the equipment and conditions needed to move a particular kind of good, such as refrigeration. Accessibility is about whether the carrier's routes reach the needed locations.

questions.stem: Emerald Gems must ship small, very high-value diamond parcels from Yellowknife to Toronto as quickly as possible. Which transportation mode fits best?
questions.explanation: Air is the fastest mode and, despite its high cost, suits small, high-value, urgent shipments. Water and rail are slower modes suited to bulky goods, and pipelines carry only liquids and gases.

questions.stem: Which statement about transportation criteria is correct?
options: Frequency is the reliability of delivery; dependability is how often shipments can be scheduled
Frequency is how often shipments can be scheduled; dependability is reliable, on-time, damage-free delivery
Accessibility is the price the carrier charges; cost is the set of routes the carrier serves
Capability is the speed of delivery; time is the availability of special equipment such as refrigeration
questions.explanation: Frequency = how often pickups or shipments can be scheduled; dependability = consistency of on-time, damage-free service. The distractors swap pairs of criteria, a common exam trick.

questions.stem: Combining transportation modes, for example moving truck trailers on railway flatcars, is called:
questions.explanation: Intermodal transportation combines two or more modes to gain the advantages of each. Cross-docking is a warehousing practice, not a transportation mode.

questions.stem: TrackMart's suppliers supply less merchandise on a more frequent basis. This is called a _____ inventory system.
questions.explanation: A just-in-time (JIT) inventory system delivers less merchandise on a more frequent basis than traditional systems, keeping inventories very low. Facilitating and transactional are channel function families, and time utility is a type of value, not an inventory system.

questions.stem: Shoreline Pharmacy lets its main supplier monitor its sales data, decide how much of each product to restock, and ship replacements automatically. This is:
questions.explanation: In vendor-managed inventory (VMI) the supplier determines the product amount and assortment a customer needs and automatically delivers it. JIT is about small, frequent deliveries; it does not require the supplier to make the reorder decision.

questions.stem: Big North Hardware's computers send purchase orders to, and receive invoices from, its suppliers' computers with no paper forms. This order-processing technology is:
questions.explanation: EDI links computers in different firms to transmit documents such as purchase orders and invoices electronically, speeding up order processing. VMI goes further by handing the reorder decision to the supplier.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between just-in-time (JIT) and vendor-managed inventory (VMI)?
options: JIT keeps stock very low with small, frequent deliveries; under VMI the supplier decides what to restock and sends it
JIT hands reorder decisions to the supplier, while VMI requires the customer to hold large safety stocks
JIT is a warehousing method with no storage time, while VMI is a mode of transportation
They are identical inventory systems that simply go by two different names
questions.explanation: JIT is defined by low inventory and frequent delivery; VMI is defined by who decides, namely the vendor. 'Warehousing with no storage' describes cross-docking, not JIT.

questions.stem: Inventory management systems designed to reduce a retailer's lead time for receiving merchandise, thereby lowering its inventory investment and improving customer service, are known as:
options: efficient consumer response or quick response systems
questions.explanation: ECR/QR systems shorten the retailer's lead time so it can carry less inventory while keeping shelves stocked. Cross-docking is a warehousing technique that may support them, but it is not the name of the inventory system.

questions.stem: What is the main risk of operating a just-in-time inventory system?
options: Inventory carrying costs become much higher than in traditional systems
Little stock on hand means a late delivery can quickly cause stockouts or stoppages
Suppliers must deliver larger shipments on a less frequent basis
It removes the need for fast, dependable transportation
questions.explanation: JIT works only with fast, on-time delivery, because there is little stock to absorb a delay. It lowers carrying costs and relies on smaller, more frequent shipments, the opposite of the distractors.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the reasons the chapter gives for holding inventory?
options: To buffer against variations in supply and demand
To speculate on future price changes
To eliminate the need for order processing
questions.explanation: Firms hold inventory to buffer variations in supply and demand, give better service, promote efficiency and speculate. Holding inventory does nothing to remove the need to process orders.

questions.stem: At a Fleetway Grocers facility, inbound trucks are unloaded and the pallets are moved straight across the dock onto outbound trucks headed to stores, spending only a few hours in the building. This practice is:
questions.explanation: Cross-docking means unloading inbound shipments and loading them onto outbound vehicles with little or no storage. A traditional storage warehouse holds goods for longer periods.

questions.stem: How does a distribution centre differ from a traditional storage warehouse?
options: A distribution centre holds goods for years, while a storage warehouse ships everything the same day
A distribution centre is always public, while a storage warehouse is always private
A distribution centre keeps goods moving; a storage warehouse holds them for longer periods
There is no difference; both are built only for long-term storage of goods
questions.explanation: Storage warehouses hold goods for moderate to long periods; distribution centres are designed to keep goods moving and often use cross-docking. Public vs private is about ownership, which is a separate warehousing decision.

questions.stem: A firm that rents space and services from an independent warehouse operator, rather than owning its own facility, is using:
questions.explanation: Public warehouses are operated by independent firms that rent space and services to others; private warehouses are owned or operated by the firm itself.

questions.stem: Harbourview Toys' volume triples for the six weeks before Christmas, and its small private warehouse is enough for the rest of the year. Which warehousing approach fits best?
options: Build a private warehouse large enough for the Christmas peak
Eliminate all warehousing and cross-dock every product year-round
Combine its private warehouse with rented public warehouse space for the peak season
Replace warehousing with a reverse logistics program
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that firms can use public, private or a combination of warehousing. Renting public space only for the peak avoids paying year-round for capacity that sits empty most of the year.

questions.stem: Which statement about warehousing is NOT correct?
options: Warehouses can be public or private
Cross-docking means storing goods for long periods before shipping them
Distribution centres are designed to facilitate the timely movement of goods
Many firms use a combination of warehousing approaches
questions.explanation: Cross-docking involves little or no storage: goods move from inbound to outbound vehicles quickly. Long-term storage describes a traditional storage warehouse.

questions.stem: Which is the BEST example of reverse logistics?
options: H&M accepts used clothing in its stores. H&M then recycles the clothing to make new textiles.
Co-op purchases products from local farmers to sell in its grocery stores.
Apple ships its products directly to customers from its online store.
Zara hosts a promotional event to launch the opening of a new store where guests are given a tote bag.
questions.explanation: Reverse logistics reclaims recyclable and reusable materials, returns and reworks from the point of consumption for repair, remanufacturing, redistribution or disposal, which is exactly what H&M does with used clothing. Apple shipping to customers is forward (outbound) logistics through a direct channel.

questions.stem: A process of reclaiming recyclable and reusable materials, returns and reworks from the point of consumption or use for repair, remanufacturing, redistribution or disposal is called:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of reverse logistics. Backward integration is a retailer or wholesaler owning upstream production; 'backward' there refers to ownership, not to products flowing back.

questions.stem: A student confuses reverse logistics with backward integration. Which explanation correctly separates them?
options: Reverse logistics moves used goods back from consumers; backward integration means owning upstream production
Reverse logistics is a retailer buying its suppliers; backward integration is recycling used products
Both terms mean returning defective goods to the manufacturer for a refund or a replacement
Reverse logistics is part of channels between nations; backward integration is part of channels within nations
questions.explanation: The two share a 'backward' feel but are unrelated: reverse logistics is the return flow of products and materials, while backward integration is ownership in a corporate VMS (e.g., a coffee chain owning its cookie bakery).

questions.stem: Voltway, an e-bike maker, collects worn batteries from customers, refurbishes the usable cells into new packs and safely disposes of the rest. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Reclaiming used products from customers for remanufacturing and disposal is reverse logistics. Backward integration would mean Voltway owning its battery supplier.

questions.stem: Why might a retailer invest in a reverse logistics program?
options: To shorten its forward channel by removing wholesalers and selling direct
To recover value from returns and used products and meet sustainability expectations
To get newly launched products to consumers faster than competitors
To gain control over its suppliers by taking ownership of them
questions.explanation: Reverse logistics turns returns and used goods into value through repair, remanufacturing, redistribution or responsible disposal, which also supports sustainability. Removing wholesalers or owning suppliers are forward-channel decisions.

questions.stem: Firms that perform most or all of the logistics functions that manufacturers, suppliers and distributors would normally perform themselves are called:
questions.explanation: Third-party logistics providers (3PLs) perform most or all logistics functions for other firms. Industrial distributors buy and resell goods, and agents negotiate sales rather than handle logistics.

questions.stem: Muskeg Apparel, an online clothing start-up, hands its warehousing, order picking, shipping and returns handling to LogiPro, an outside firm that does the same for dozens of other brands. LogiPro is a:
questions.explanation: An outside firm performing most or all logistics functions for other companies is a 3PL. A strategic channel alliance would involve selling Muskeg's products through another firm's marketing channel, not outsourcing its logistics.

questions.stem: How does a third-party logistics provider typically differ from a wholesaler?
options: A 3PL always takes title to the goods it handles, whereas a wholesaler never does
A 3PL sells mainly to final consumers, whereas a wholesaler sells only to manufacturers
A 3PL stores and moves goods for a fee without buying them; a wholesaler takes title and resells
The two terms are interchangeable, since both store and move goods for other firms
questions.explanation: A 3PL is a logistics service firm that moves and stores other firms' goods. A wholesaler buys (takes title to) goods and resells them, performing transactional as well as logistical functions.

questions.stem: Why would a manufacturer outsource its logistics to a 3PL?
options: A specialist can do the work more efficiently, letting the manufacturer focus on its core business
Outsourcing removes the need for any logistics functions to be performed at all
A 3PL guarantees the manufacturer exclusive distribution in each of its markets
A 3PL takes ownership of the manufacturer's retail customers and their accounts
questions.explanation: Like any channel partner, a 3PL must add value by doing the work better or more cheaply. The functions still have to be performed; outsourcing only changes who performs them.

questions.stem: Which task would a third-party logistics provider be LEAST likely to perform for a client?
options: Designing the client's national advertising campaign
questions.explanation: 3PLs handle logistics functions such as warehousing, transportation, order fulfilment and returns. Advertising is a promotion activity outside logistics.
